sentence: ENO and WENO schemes are high order accurate finite difference schemes designed for problems with piecewise smooth solutions containing discontinuities.

scheme.definition: Conservative semi-discrete scheme du_i/dt = -(1/Δx_i)(f^_{i+1/2} - f^_{i-1/2}) (2.68) (finite volume) or du_i/dt = -(1/Δx)(f^_{i+1/2} - f^_{i-1/2}) (2.73) (finite difference), with the numerical flux built from the adaptive-stencil ENO reconstruction (Procedure 2.1: start from a two-point stencil and add one cell at a time on the side with the smaller absolute divided difference, giving a polynomial of degree at most k-1) or the WENO reconstruction (Procedure 2.2: convex combination of the k candidate-stencil reconstructions with nonlinear weights ω_r built from smoothness indicators β_r, giving a (2k-1)-th order reconstruction), together with a monotone flux (2.70)-(2.72) or a flux splitting (2.75), and a time discretization from Sect. 4.2.
scheme.location: Procedure 2.1, p. 14; Procedure 2.2, pp. 19-20; schemes (2.68) p. 20 and (2.73) p. 22; Sect. 2.3

hypotheses.hypothesis: Accuracy is stated for smooth regions: ENO interpolation P_i(x) = V(x) + O(Δx^{k+1}) in any cell not containing a discontinuity; WENO gives (2k-1)-th order accuracy in smooth regions
hypotheses.location: p. 15, Property 1; p. 16; Procedure 2.2 step 5, p. 20

hypotheses.hypothesis: Finite difference version of third or higher order only on a uniform or smoothly varying grid

justification: 'High order accurate' gives no order and no norm. The notes establish formal order only (reconstruction / truncation error, pp. 15-20) and prove no convergence rate; they also say free stencil adaptation 'may cause loss of accuracy when applied to a hyperbolic PDE [63, 67]' (p. 16). Shu 1990 (ICASE Report 90-55, Introduction, source shu_1990_eno_accuracy pdf p. 5) says a convergence theory for ENO is not available, and reports (pdf p. 6) that the third order ENO scheme for u_t + u_x = 0 with u0 = sin^4(πx) reaches only about 1.97 order in L1. Henrick, Aslam and Powers, J. Comput. Phys. 207 (2005), abstract (source henrick_aslam_powers_2005_mapped), show the Jiang-Shu fifth order WENO is in general only third order at critical points. Whether such reduced rates still count as 'high order' depends on a threshold the sentence does not give, so both readings are UNSURE.

sentence: The Runge-Kutta method (4.8) is TVD under the CFL coefficient (4.7): c = min_{i,k} α_{ik}/β_{ik}, (4.9) provided that α_{ik} ≥ 0, β_{ik} ≥ 0.

scheme.definition: General m-stage Runge-Kutta method (4.8): u^{(i)} = sum_{k=0}^{i-1} ( α_{ik} u^{(k)} + Δt β_{ik} L(u^{(k)}) ), i = 1,...,m; u^{(0)} = u^n, u^{(m)} = u^{n+1}; by consistency sum_{k=0}^{i-1} α_{ik} = 1. L is the spatial operator of the method of lines u_t = L(u) (4.2), e.g. an ENO or WENO approximation of -f(u)_x.

hypotheses.hypothesis: u_t = L(u) (4.2) is a method-of-lines approximation of u_t = -f(u)_x (4.3); the discussion applies in any spatial dimension

First order Euler forward u^{n+1} = u^n + Δt L(u^n) (4.4) is stable in a certain norm, ||u^{n+1}|| ≤ ||u^n|| (4.5) (total variation for 'TVD'), under Δt ≤ Δt_1 (4.6); the high order method should keep (4.5) under Δt ≤ c Δt_1 (4.7)

justification: With hypotheses: the argument just before the lemma (p. 43) is that with nonnegative coefficients each stage is a convex combination (sum α_{ik} = 1) of forward Euler steps with step (β_{ik}/α_{ik})Δt, so (4.5) carries over when Δt ≤ c Δt_1. The same result is Lemma 2.1 of Gottlieb, Shu and Tadmor, 'Strong stability-preserving high-order time discretization methods', SIAM Review 43 (2001), p. 92 (source gottlieb_shu_tadmor_2001_ssp), and Lemma 1.1 of Gottlieb and Shu 1998 (source gottlieb_shu_1998_tvdrk). Alone: the sentence carries the sign condition, and 'under the CFL coefficient (4.7)' means Δt ≤ c Δt_1 with Δt_1 defined as the forward Euler stable step (4.6), so the forward Euler hypothesis is built into the sentence's own reference; TRUE. (If some α_{ik} = 0 with β_{ik} > 0 then c = 0 and the claim is vacuous.)

sentence: The Runge-Kutta method (4.8) is TVD under the CFL coefficient (4.7): c = min_{i,k} α_{ik}/|β_{ik}|, (4.14) provided that α_{ik} ≥ 0, and L is replaced by L~ for negative β_{ik}.

scheme.definition: General m-stage Runge-Kutta method (4.8): u^{(i)} = sum_{k=0}^{i-1} ( α_{ik} u^{(k)} + Δt β_{ik} L(u^{(k)}) ), i = 1,...,m; u^{(0)} = u^n, u^{(m)} = u^{n+1}; sum_{k=0}^{i-1} α_{ik} = 1; for negative β_{ik}, L is replaced by the adjoint operator L~ of (4.12).

hypotheses.hypothesis: u_t = L(u) (4.2) is a method-of-lines approximation of u_t = -f(u)_x (4.3); the discussion applies in any spatial dimension

First order Euler forward u^{n+1} = u^n + Δt L(u^n) (4.4) is stable in a certain norm, ||u^{n+1}|| ≤ ||u^n|| (4.5) (total variation for 'TVD'), under Δt ≤ Δt_1 (4.6); the high order method should keep (4.5) under Δt ≤ c Δt_1 (4.7)

L~ approximates the same spatial derivative(s) as L but is TVD (or stable in another relevant norm) for first order Euler backward in time, u^{n+1} = u^n - Δt L~(u^n) (4.12); for conservation laws obtained by solving u_t = f(u)_x (4.13), i.e. reversing the upwind direction. The time-step restriction for (4.12) is not stated; read here as the same Δt ≤ Δt_1.

justification: With hypotheses: the convex-combination argument of Lemma 4.1 goes through with, for negative β_{ik}, the backward Euler step u - |β_{ik}|Δt L~(u), stable by the requirement on L~ (p. 44). The same result, with the backward Euler stability of L~ stated explicitly under the same CFL restriction, is Lemma 2.2 of Gottlieb, Shu and Tadmor, SIAM Review 43 (2001), p. 93 (source gottlieb_shu_tadmor_2001_ssp). Alone: the sentence names L~, which the notes define by that stability requirement, and (4.7) refers to Δt_1; TRUE under that reading. Caveat: the notes never state the step restriction for backward Euler with L~; if it were smaller than Δt_1, the c in (4.14) would be too large, so both TRUE values rest on reading it as Δt_1, as the 2001 paper makes explicit.

sentence: The multi-step method (4.23) is TVD under the CFL coefficient (4.7): c = min_k α_k/β_k, (4.24) provided that α_k ≥ 0, β_k ≥ 0.

scheme.definition: General multi-step method (4.23): u^{n+1} = sum_{k=0}^{m} ( α_k u^{n-k} + Δt β_k L(u^{n-k}) ), with sum_{k=0}^{m} α_k = 1 by consistency; L is the spatial operator of the method of lines u_t = L(u) (4.2).

hypotheses.hypothesis: u_t = L(u) (4.2) is a method-of-lines approximation of u_t = -f(u)_x (4.3)
First order Euler forward (4.4) is stable in a certain norm (4.5) under Δt ≤ Δt_1 (4.6); the multi-step method should keep (4.5) under Δt ≤ c Δt_1 (4.7)

justification: Counterexample to the literal claim (same as for Lemma 2.3 of Gottlieb, Shu and Tadmor 2001, see gottlieb_shu_tadmor_2001_ssp items): the notes define the property sought for multi-step methods as (4.5), ||u^{n+1}|| <= ||u^n|| (pp. 42 and 47). Take the three-step method u^{n+1} = (3/4)u^n + (1/4)u^{n-2} + (3/2)Δt L(u^n) (alpha = (3/4, 0, 1/4), beta = (3/2, 0, 0), all >= 0, c = 1/2; scheme 2 of Table 5.1 in Gottlieb-Shu-Tadmor 2001) and L(u) = -u on grid functions, for which forward Euler is TVD for Δt <= Δt_1 = 2. With Δt = c Δt_1 = 1 and exact starting values (TV scaled by 1, e^{-1}, e^{-2}) the next level has TV scaled by 1/4 - (3/4)e^{-2} ≈ 0.1485 > e^{-2} ≈ 0.1353, so TV(u^{n+1}) > TV(u^n). The convex-combination argument (p. 47) only gives TV(u^{n+1}) <= max_k TV(u^{n-k}), a weaker property than (4.5). This counterexample is our own hand computation, not taken from a published source.

sentence: It was shown by Liu et al. that WENO schemes constructed from the r th order (in L1 norm) ENO schemes are (r+1) th order accurate.

scheme.definition: Finite difference WENO scheme of Liu, Osher and Chan in the flux (point-value) form: du_j/dt = L(u), L = -(1/Δx)(f^_{j+1/2} - f^_{j-1/2}) (2.2); split flux f = f^+ + f^- (2.4), e.g. global Lax-Friedrichs f^±(u) = (1/2)(f(u) ± αu), α = max|f'(u)| (2.5); f^_{j+1/2} = sum_{k=0}^{r-1} ω_k q^r_k(f_{j+k-r+1}, ..., f_{j+k}) (2.10), q^r_k(g_0,...,g_{r-1}) = sum_l a^r_{k,l} g_l (2.8) with the coefficients of Table 1; weights ω_k = α_k/(α_0+...+α_{r-1}) (2.15), α_k = C^r_k/(ε + IS_k)^p (2.16), optimal weights C^r_k of Table 2 (r=3: 1/10, 6/10, 3/10), ε > 0 (10^-6 in the tests), p = 2 in the tests; original smoothness measurement IS_k = sum_{l=1}^{r-1} sum_{i=1}^{r-l} (f[j+k+i-r, l])^2/(r-l) (2.18) with f[.,l] the l-th undivided difference. Time stepping: third order TVD Runge-Kutta RK-3 (1.3) or classical RK-4 (1.4).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Order holds in smooth monotone regions of f(u(x)), i.e. f' ≠ 0 (Taylor expansion (2.21)-(2.22))
At critical points of f(u(x)) the r = 3 scheme of Liu et al. is only 3rd order accurate
Order measured as truncation error of the spatial operator for smooth solutions; ε treated as negligible in the expansion

justification: Alone: the sentence claims (r+1)th order with no restriction, but the same paper (p. 7, after (2.25)) states that because (2.22) fails at critical points of f(u(x)) the r = 3 scheme of Liu et al. is only 3rd order there (not 4th); so the unrestricted claim is false. With hypotheses: in smooth monotone regions (f' ≠ 0) the Taylor analysis (2.21)-(2.22) gives ω_k = C^r_k + O(h) and hence (r+1)th order (p. 7; summary p. 8), matching Liu et al.; Henrick, Aslam and Powers 2005 (Table 1, p. 552) confirm that the indicators behave regularly when f' ≠ 0.

sentence: We propose a new way of measuring the smoothness of a numerical solution, emulating the idea of minimizing the total variation of the approximation, which results in a 5th order WENO scheme for the case r = 3, instead of the 4th order with the original smoothness measurement by Liu et al.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Smooth regions with f' ≠ 0: IS_k = (f'h)^2(1 + O(h^2)) (3.8), giving (2.17) and 5th order
The source additionally claims 5th order at critical points (f' = 0) from (3.9)
Original measurement gives 4th order (r+1) only in smooth monotone regions
ε treated as negligible in the order analysis

justification: Alone (5th order for smooth solutions in general, which the source explicitly intends, p. 9 eq. (3.9)): Henrick, Aslam and Powers 2005 (J. Comput. Phys. 207, abstract p. 542, Sec. 4.2 eq. (39) and Table 1 p. 552, Tables 3 and 8) show that the Jiang-Shu weights satisfy only ω_k = ω̄_k + O(Δx) at critical points where f' = 0 and f''' ≠ 0, so the scheme is only 3rd order there (when ε does not dominate the indicators); they also note the discrepancy with (3.5), (3.7), (3.9). With the hypothesis f' ≠ 0 stated for (3.8): the indicators satisfy (2.17), the weights are C_k + O(h^2), and the scheme is 5th order (confirmed by HAP Table 1, f' ≠ 0 column); the original measurement gives 4th order there (p. 7), so the comparison part holds as well.

sentence: We also prove that, for conservation laws with smooth solutions, all WENO schemes are convergent.

scheme.definition: WENO schemes (2.2), (2.10), (2.15)-(2.16) with smoothness measurement (2.18) or (3.1), any r ≥ 2, with a smooth flux splitting (e.g. global Lax-Friedrichs (2.5)), time-discretized by Runge-Kutta methods.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Scalar conservation laws (m = 1)
Exact solution v and df/dv, g have r + [(d+1)/2] + q_0 + 2 continuous derivatives in the domain of dependence
Smooth flux splitting (e.g. global Lax-Friedrichs)
n-th order Runge-Kutta time stepping with n ≥ max(r, 3)
hypotheses.location: Theorem 6.1, p. 15; p. 15 (3rd or higher order RK)

hypotheses.hypothesis: Appropriately chosen CFL number (Table 5: r=2: 1.625 (n=3), 1.745 (n=4); r=3: 1.434, 1.731)

justification: Alone ('all WENO schemes', any time stepping, any time step): Wang and Spiteri, 'Linear instability of the fifth-order WENO method', SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 45 (2007) (abstract and Theorems 3.1, 3.4) show WENO5 with forward Euler and with every two-stage second-order explicit RK method is linearly unstable and hence not convergent; Motamed, Macdonald and Ruuth (2010/11, abstract, p. 12) find forward Euler stable only for time steps with CFL number of order θ^4 ~ Δx^4, i.e. no fixed CFL number works. So the dropped time-stepping/CFL hypotheses are needed. With hypotheses: the argument (pp. 14-15) only computes the spectrum of the first variation at a constant state (frozen weights C_k) and then says 'the same analysis gives' Theorem 6.1 via Strang's theorem; l2 stability of the first variation about a non-constant smooth solution is not shown, so the proof is only sketched. Wang-Spiteri (p. 3) do confirm linear stability of WENO5 with three-stage third-order and four-stage fourth-order RK, consistent with the hypotheses, but nothing we read completes the proof.

sentence: For the initial value problem of (1.1) with m = 1 (i.e., scalar conservation laws), ∀ (x0, t0) ∈ R^d × R+, if the exact solution v and df/dv, g have r + [(d+1)/2] + q0 + 2 continuous derivatives in the domain of dependence of (x0, t0) as defined in [18], the WENO schemes using a smooth flux splitting and a n th order Runge-Kutta scheme (n ≥ max(r, 3)) satisfy u(x0, t0; Δx) = v(x0, t0) + O(Δx^r) (6.5) for appropriately chosen CFL number.

scheme.definition: WENO schemes with spatial operator L = L(f_{j-r}, ..., f_{j+r-1}) (6.1) built from (2.2), (2.10), (2.15), (2.16) and (2.18) or (3.1), r ≥ 2 the L1 order of the base ENO scheme, smooth flux splitting (e.g. global Lax-Friedrichs (2.5)), time-discretized by an n-th order Runge-Kutta method; ε > 0 in (2.16) makes L infinitely differentiable.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Scalar (m = 1), d space dimensions, forcing term g allowed
v and df/dv, g have r + [(d+1)/2] + q0 + 2 continuous derivatives in the domain of dependence; q0 a small constant integer from Strang [18]
Smooth flux splitting
Runge-Kutta of order n ≥ max(r, 3)
Appropriately chosen (fixed) CFL number, examples in Table 5

justification: The sentence carries its own hypotheses, so both readings coincide. The proof (pp. 14-15) shows only that the first variation linearized at a constant state, where ∂ω_k/∂u_l = 0 and ω_k = C^r_k, has spectrum in the left half plane (6.3)-(6.4), and then states that 'the same analysis gives' the theorem through Strang's theorem; Strang's theorem needs l2 stability of the first variation about the actual smooth solution, which is not verified, so the proof is a sketch. The O(Δx^r) truncation part is consistent with Henrick et al. 2005 (Sec. 6, Table 10: rates ≥ r for r = 3 at f' = 0 with ε negligible), but for r = 2 Table 10 gives rate 1 at critical points when ε is negligible; with fixed ε > 0 the weights tend to the optimal ones as Δx → 0 (HAP p. 553), so this is not a refutation. Linear stability with RK3/RK4 under a CFL limit is consistent with Wang-Spiteri 2007 (p. 3). Nothing we read settles the full claim.

sentence: With the new smooth measurement, which is based on minimizing the L2 norm of the derivatives of the interpolation polynomials, the WENO schemes formulated from the r th order ENO schemes can be made (2r-1) th order accurate in smooth regions of the flux function (in spatial variables), at least for r = 2, 3.

scheme.definition: WENO scheme (2.2), (2.10), (2.15)-(2.16) with the new smoothness measurement (3.1) (for r = 2 identical to (2.18), i.e. IS_k = (f[j+k-1, 1])^2 (2.19); for r = 3 given by (3.2)-(3.4)); optimal weights C^r_k of Table 2; ε > 0 (10^-6 in tests), p = 2.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Smooth regions; for r = 3 the 5th order derivation uses f' ≠ 0 ((3.8))
The source also asserts 5th order at critical points via (3.9)
For r = 2 the optimal 3rd order is reached in smooth monotone regions ('in most smooth regions')
ε treated as negligible in the order analysis

justification: Alone ('in smooth regions', which includes critical points of f): Henrick, Aslam and Powers 2005 show that with these weights the r = 3 scheme is only 3rd order at critical points with f' = 0, f''' ≠ 0 (abstract p. 542; eq. (39), p. 552; Tables 3 and 8), and their Sec. 6 / Table 10 (p. 565-566) gives rate 1 for r = 2 and rate 3 for r = 3 at first-order critical points (ε negligible); so (2r-1)th order fails in part of the smooth region. With the hypothesis f' ≠ 0 (stated for (3.8), and p. 7 for r = 2): the indicators satisfy (2.17), the weights are C_k + O(h^{r-1}), and the scheme is (2r-1)th order (HAP Table 1, f' ≠ 0; Table 10, n_CP = 0 rates 3 and 5).

sentence: However, at discontinuities, all WENO schemes are just r th accurate (r is the order of the base ENO scheme).

scheme.definition: WENO schemes (2.2), (2.10), (2.15)-(2.16) with smoothness measurement (2.18) or (3.1), base ENO order r, p = 2, ε > 0.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Near a discontinuity at least one candidate stencil is smooth; IS = O(h^2) on smooth stencils (2.26) and O(1) on non-smooth ones (2.27), so non-smooth stencils get weight O(h^{2p}) (2.28)

justification: Alone (accuracy at a discontinuity): no shock-capturing scheme is r-th order accurate across a discontinuity; Henrick et al. 2005 (pp. 564-565, Table 9; p. 566) report L1 rates of roughly 5/6 to 1 for both WENO5 variants on the Sod problem and state that any shock-capturing scheme drops to at most first order for discontinuous flows. With the hypothesis that the claim means grid points near a discontinuity whose stencils include smooth ones: the source gives only the heuristic weight estimates (2.26)-(2.28), and itself notes that at the point next to the discontinuity the weights 'do not approximate a 4th order scheme' (pp. 9-10), with no proof of r-th order; nothing we read settles it.

sentence: We illustrate with numerical examples that non-TVD but linearly stable Runge-Kutta time discretization can generate oscillations even for TVD (total variation diminishing) spatial discretization, verifying the claim that TVD Runge-Kutta methods are important for such applications.

scheme.definition: Non-TVD but linearly stable Runge-Kutta time discretization; the example used is the two-stage second order method (2.5): u^(1) = u^n − 20ΔtL(u^n), u^{n+1} = u^n + (41/40)ΔtL(u^n) − (1/40)ΔtL(u^(1)). TVD spatial discretization: conservative difference (1/Δx)(f̂_{j+1/2} − f̂_{j−1/2}) with f̂_{j+1/2} = h(u^−_{j+1/2}, u^+_{j+1/2}), u^−_{j+1/2} = u_j + (1/2)minmod(u_{j+1} − u_j, u_j − u_{j−1}), u^+_{j+1/2} = u_{j+1} − (1/2)minmod(u_{j+2} − u_{j+1}, u_{j+1} − u_j), h the Godunov flux, minmod(a,b) = ((sign(a)+sign(b))/2) min(|a|,|b|); Euler forward with it is TVD under Δt ≤ Δx/(2 max_j |u^n_j|) (2.3).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Burgers equation u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 with Riemann data u = 1 for x ≤ 0, u = −0.5 for x > 0
time step Δt = Δx/(2 max_j |u^n_j|)

justification: The claim is existential and is supported only by the computation in Fig. 1 (p. 77): with the minmod MUSCL / Godunov spatial operator, method (2.5) gives an overshoot for the Burgers Riemann problem while the TVD method (2.4) does not. That (2.5) has negative β's in both stages (p. 76) is clear, but the oscillation itself is numerical evidence, not a proof; the same example is reproduced in Gottlieb–Shu–Tadmor 2001, Fig. 2.1 (p. 91), still only numerically. The second clause ('important for such applications') has no definite truth value. Same status alone and with hypotheses.

sentence: The Runge-Kutta method (1.8) is TVD under the CFL coefficient (1.7): c = min_{i,k} α_ik/β_ik, (1.9) provided that α_ik ≥ 0, β_ik ≥ 0.

scheme.definition: General m-stage Runge-Kutta method (1.8): u^(i) = Σ_{k=0}^{i−1} (α_ik u^(k) + Δt β_ik L(u^(k))), i = 1, ..., m; u^(0) = u^n, u^(m) = u^{n+1}; consistency Σ_{k=0}^{i−1} α_ik = 1. Applied to u_t = L(u) (1.1), where −L(u) is a TVD approximation of f(u)_x: TV(u^{n+1}) ≤ TV(u^n) (1.4), TV(u) = Σ_j |u_{j+1} − u_j| (1.3), for Euler forward u^{n+1} = u^n + ΔtL(u^n) (1.5) under Δt ≤ Δt_1 (1.6). hypotheses.hypothesis: Euler forward (1.5) with the spatial operator L is TVD under Δt ≤ Δt_1
consistency Σ_k α_ik = 1
α_ik ≥ 0, β_ik ≥ 0

justification: With hypotheses: p. 74 gives the argument: with nonnegative coefficients and Σ_k α_ik = 1, each stage is a convex combination of Euler forward steps with Δt replaced by (β_ik/α_ik)Δt, and TV is convex, so each stage (and u^{n+1}) is TVD when (β_ik/α_ik)Δt ≤ Δt_1 for all i,k, i.e. Δt ≤ cΔt_1. The argument is complete (ratios with β_ik = 0 count as +∞). Alone: the sentence itself contains the nonnegativity condition and the CFL coefficient; the assumption that Euler forward is TVD is carried by Δt_1 in (1.7), which (1.6) defines as the Euler forward TVD step, so nothing needed is dropped.

sentence: The Runge-Kutta method (1.8) is TVD under the CFL coefficient (1.7): c = min_{i,k} α_ik/|β_ik|, (1.12) provided that α_ik ≥ 0, and L is replaced by L̃ for negative β_ik.

scheme.definition: General m-stage Runge-Kutta method (1.8) (see Lemma 1.1 item), with βL replaced by βL̃ whenever β_ik < 0, where the adjoint operator L̃ approximates the same spatial derivative(s) as L but is TVD for first order Euler backward in time u^{n+1} = u^n − ΔtL̃(u^n) (1.10); for conservation laws L̃ is obtained from the backward-in-time problem u_t = f(u)_x (1.11), i.e. by changing the upwind direction.

Euler backward in time with L̃, u^{n+1} = u^n − ΔtL̃(u^n), is TVD (under the same step restriction)

Alone: the sentence states α_ik ≥ 0 and the replacement of L by L̃; the TVD requirements on L (through Δt_1 in (1.7)) and on L̃ are part of how L and L̃ are defined in the text (pp. 73–74), so no needed hypothesis is dropped.

sentence: If we require α_ik ≥ 0 and β_ik ≥ 0, then the optimal second order TVD Runge-Kutta method (1.8) is given by u^(1) = u^n + ΔtL(u^n), (3.2) u^{n+1} = (1/2)u^n + (1/2)u^(1) + (1/2)ΔtL(u^(1)), with a CFL coefficient c = 1 in (1.9).

hypotheses.hypothesis: m-stage, m-th order methods with m = 2 (section 3 looks at m-stage, m-th order methods written in the form (1.8))
α_ik ≥ 0, β_ik ≥ 0; CFL coefficient measured by (1.9)
Euler forward with L TVD under Δt ≤ Δt_1

justification: With hypotheses (two stages): the proof on p. 78 shows c > 1 forces β_20 < 0; (3.2) has α_10/β_10 = 1, α_21/β_21 = 1, β_20 = 0, α_20 = 1/2, so c = 1 is attained, and from (3.1) c = 1 forces β_10 = 1, α_21 = 1/2, so (3.2) is the only such method. Alone: the sentence does not restrict the number of stages, and with more stages a second order method of form (1.8) with nonnegative coefficients beats c = 1. Hand-checked example: u^(1) = u^n + (1/2)ΔtL(u^n), u^(2) = u^(1) + (1/2)ΔtL(u^(1)), u^{n+1} = (1/3)u^n + (2/3)u^(2) + (1/3)ΔtL(u^(2)); its Butcher weights b = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3), nodes (0, 1/2, 1) satisfy Σb = 1, Σbc = 1/2 (second order), and every ratio α/β equals 2, so c = 2 in (1.9).

sentence: If we require α_ik ≥ 0 and β_ik ≥ 0, then the optimal third order TVD Runge-Kutta method (1.8) is given by u^(1) = u^n + ΔtL(u^n), u^(2) = (3/4)u^n + (1/4)u^(1) + (1/4)ΔtL(u^(1)), (3.3) u^{n+1} = (1/3)u^n + (2/3)u^(2) + (2/3)ΔtL(u^(2)), with a CFL coefficient c = 1 in (1.9).

α_ik ≥ 0, β_ik ≥ 0; CFL coefficient measured by (1.9)

justification: With hypotheses (three stages): the Appendix (pp. 81–83) runs through Ralston's general case and special cases and shows c > 1 is impossible. sentence: The four stage, fourth order Runge-Kutta scheme (1.8) with a nonzero CFL coefficient c in (1.12) must have at least one negative β_ik.

scheme.definition: Four-stage form of (1.8), u^(i) = Σ_{k=0}^{i−1} (α_ik u^(k) + Δtβ_ik L(u^(k))), with fourth order accuracy (Butcher form (5.1)–(5.2), Ralston's families); CFL coefficient (1.12) c = min α_ik/|β_ik| with α_ik ≥ 0 and L̃ used for negative β_ik.

hypotheses.hypothesis: all α_ik ≥ 0 (needed for the TVD criterion)
fourth order accuracy for general (nonlinear) ODEs

justification: With hypotheses: the Appendix (pp. 83–84) shows that nonnegative β_ik imply nonnegative Butcher coefficients c_ik via (5.2), and the case analysis over the general and special fourth order families rules out all nonnegative c_ik, except classical RK4, where α_21 = −2β_20 forces c = 0. The result is restated as Proposition 4.2 of Gottlieb–Shu–Tadmor 2001 (p. 101). Alone: the sentence carries the needed conditions (nonzero c in (1.12) presupposes α_ik ≥ 0). 'Fourth order' is read in the usual sense (all ODEs); if read as fourth order only for linear L it would fail, since the four-stage method (3.1)–(3.2) of Gottlieb–Shu–Tadmor 2001 (p. 95) is linearly fourth order with all β ≥ 0 and c = 1.

sentence: While for second and third order optimal methods are found with a CFL coefficient equal to one, for fourth order we simply give the best method we can find.

scheme.definition: Optimal TVD Runge-Kutta methods of form (1.8): second order (3.2) and third order (3.3), each with c = 1 in (1.9); fourth order best found (3.4) with c = 0.936 in (1.12) using two L̃ evaluations.

hypotheses.hypothesis: m-stage, m-th order methods, m = 2, 3, 4
α_ik ≥ 0 and β_ik ≥ 0 for m = 2, 3

justification: With hypotheses: Propositions 3.1 and 3.2 (proofs p. 78 and Appendix pp. 81–83) show that c = 1 is optimal for two-stage second order and three-stage third order methods with nonnegative coefficients; the fourth order part only reports the best method found (p. 79, which explicitly makes no optimality claim). Alone: without the restriction to m stages, the 'optimal' second and third order methods do not have c = 1: a three-stage second order method and a four-stage third order method with nonnegative coefficients and c = 2 exist (both written out and hand-checked in items :04 and :05).

sentence: A TVD third order low storage Runge-Kutta method is found, which uses only two storage units per equation and has a CFL coefficient equal to 0.32.

scheme.definition: Low storage form (4.1): du^(i) = A_i du^(i−1) + ΔtL(u^(i−1)), u^(i) = u^(i−1) + B_i du^(i), i = 1, ..., m, u^(0) = u^n, u^(m) = u^{n+1}, A_0 = 0; Carpenter–Kennedy three-stage third order one-parameter family (4.2) (B_1 = c_2, B_2, B_3, A_2, A_3 given through z_1, ..., z_6), with c_2 = 0.924574 (4.3).

Euler forward with L TVD under Δt ≤ Δt_1

justification: Third order and two storage units follow from the Carpenter–Kennedy family (4.2) and the form (4.1) (p. 79). The TVD property with c = 0.32 comes from a computer search; the text says 'The result seems to indicate that c_2 = 0.924574 gives an almost best choice, with CFL coefficient c = 0.32 in (1.9)' (p. 80), and the three conversion parameters to form (1.8) are not printed, so the nonnegativity of the α's and β's and the value 0.32 cannot be checked from what we read. Same status alone.

sentence: Finally, we prove that general four stage fourth order Runge-Kutta methods cannot be TVD without introducing an adjoint operator L̃.

scheme.definition: General four-stage fourth order Runge-Kutta method in form (1.8) / Butcher form (5.1); TVD in the sense of Lemmas 1.1–1.2 (nonnegative α_ik, CFL coefficient (1.9) or (1.12)).

hypotheses.hypothesis: TVD established through the criterion of Lemma 1.1 (α_ik ≥ 0, β_ik ≥ 0) with positive CFL coefficient
L general (nonlinear); fourth order for general ODEs

justification: With hypotheses: this is Proposition 3.3 (Appendix, pp. 83–84): any four-stage fourth order method with positive c in (1.12) has a negative β_ik, so the criterion of Lemma 1.1 cannot be met without L̃. The paper proves only that its sufficient criterion fails, not that TV must increase for some L. Alone: for linear L the claim fails. Gottlieb–Shu–Tadmor 2001, eq. (3.5) (p. 96), writes classical RK4 as the convex combination 3/8 + (1/3)(I+ΔtL) + (1/4)(I+ΔtL)^2 + (1/24)(I+ΔtL)^4, so it is TVD with c = 1 whenever Euler forward is, with no L̃.

sentence: Previously termed TVD (total variation diminishing) time discretizations, these high-order time discretization methods preserve the strong stability properties of first-order Euler time stepping and have proved very useful, especially in solving hyperbolic partial differential equations.

scheme.definition: SSP (strong stability-preserving) explicit time discretizations of d/dt u = L(u) (2.1): Runge–Kutta (2.9) u^(0) = u^n, u^(i) = Σ_{k=0}^{i−1} (α_{i,k}u^(k) + Δtβ_{i,k}L(u^(k))), α_{i,k} ≥ 0, u^{n+1} = u^(m); multistep (2.14) u^{n+1} = Σ_{i=1}^m (α_i u^{n+1−i} + Δtβ_i L(u^{n+1−i})), α_i ≥ 0; with L̃ in place of L for negative β. Forward Euler (2.3) u^{n+1} = u^n + ΔtL(u^n) is assumed strongly stable, ‖u^n + ΔtL(u^n)‖ ≤ ‖u^n‖, under Δt ≤ Δt_FE (2.4); SSP means the same norm bound under Δt ≤ cΔt_FE (2.6). Implicit versions: section 6.

hypotheses.hypothesis: forward Euler strongly stable in the norm (or convex functional) under Δt ≤ Δt_FE
time step Δt ≤ cΔt_FE with c from (2.10), (2.13) or (2.15)
α ≥ 0, β ≥ 0, or L̃ (strongly stable for backward-in-time Euler) used for negative β

justification: With hypotheses: Lemmas 2.1–2.3 (pp. 92–93) prove it by writing each stage or step as a convex combination of forward Euler steps. For multistep methods the bound that is actually preserved is ‖u^{n+1}‖ ≤ max_i ‖u^{n+1−i}‖ (see item :04). Alone: the sentence drops the reduced step Δt ≤ cΔt_FE, and that restriction is needed. Hand-checked: scheme 2 of Table 5.1 (p. 105; three-step, α = (3/4, 0, 1/4), β = (3/2, 0, 0), c = 1/2) with L(u) = −u and Δt = Δt_FE = 2 (forward Euler factor |1−Δt| = 1, non-expansive) gives u^{n+1} = −(9/4)u^n + (1/4)u^{n−2}, whose characteristic polynomial r^3 + (9/4)r^2 − 1/4 has a root near r = −2.2. Solutions therefore grow without bound. 'Have proved very useful' has no truth value and does not change this.

sentence: If the forward Euler method (2.3) is strongly stable under the CFL restriction (2.4), ‖u^n + ΔtL(u^n)‖ ≤ ‖u^n‖, then the Runge–Kutta method (2.9) with β_{i,k} ≥ 0 is SSP, ‖u^{n+1}‖ ≤ ‖u^n‖, provided the following CFL restriction (2.6) is fulfilled: Δt ≤ cΔt_FE, c = min_{i,k} α_{i,k}/β_{i,k}. (2.10)

scheme.definition: General m-stage Runge–Kutta method (2.9): u^(0) = u^n, u^(i) = Σ_{k=0}^{i−1} (α_{i,k}u^(k) + Δtβ_{i,k}L(u^(k))), α_{i,k} ≥ 0, i = 1, ..., m, u^{n+1} = u^(m); consistency Σ_{k=0}^{i−1} α_{i,k} = 1.

hypotheses.hypothesis: forward Euler strongly stable under Δt ≤ Δt_FE
‖·‖ a norm (the argument uses only convexity, so any convex functional)

justification: With hypotheses: p. 92 shows each stage u^(i) is a convex combination of forward Euler steps with Δt replaced by (β_{i,k}/α_{i,k})Δt; by the triangle inequality and induction over the stages, ‖u^(i)‖ ≤ ‖u^n‖ when Δt ≤ cΔt_FE. The argument is complete (β = 0 terms impose no restriction). Alone: the sentence states every hypothesis it needs (Euler strong stability, β ≥ 0, the CFL restriction), and α ≥ 0 is part of (2.9).

sentence: If the forward Euler method combined with the spatial discretization L in (2.3) is strongly stable under the CFL restriction (2.4), ‖u^n + ΔtL(u^n)‖ ≤ ‖u^n‖, and if Euler’s method solved backward in time in combination with the spatial discretization L̃ in (2.11) is also strongly stable under the CFL restriction (2.4), ‖u^n − ΔtL̃(u^n)‖ ≤ ‖u^n‖, then the Runge–Kutta method (2.9) is SSP, ‖u^{n+1}‖ ≤ ‖u^n‖, under the CFL restriction (2.6), Δt ≤ cΔt_FE, c = min_{i,k} α_{i,k}/|β_{i,k}|, (2.13) provided β_{i,k}L is replaced by β_{i,k}L̃ whenever β_{i,k} is negative.

scheme.definition: Runge–Kutta method (2.9) (α_{i,k} ≥ 0, Σ_k α_{i,k} = 1) with β_{i,k}L replaced by β_{i,k}L̃ for negative β_{i,k}; L̃ approximates the same spatial derivative(s) as L and is strongly stable for backward-in-time Euler u^{n+1} = u^n − ΔtL̃(u^n) (2.11); for conservation laws obtained from u_t = f(u)_x (2.12) by changing the upwind direction.

hypotheses.hypothesis: forward Euler with L and backward-in-time Euler with L̃ both strongly stable under Δt ≤ Δt_FE

justification: With hypotheses: the convex-combination argument of p. 92 applies term by term; a term α_{i,k}u^(k) + Δtβ_{i,k}L̃(u^(k)) with β < 0 is α_{i,k} times a backward-in-time Euler step with step (|β_{i,k}|/α_{i,k})Δt ≤ Δt_FE, which is non-expansive by hypothesis. The sentence states all its hypotheses, so the status alone is the same.

sentence: If the forward Euler method combined with the spatial discretization L in (2.3) is strongly stable under the CFL restriction (2.4), ‖u^n + ΔtL(u^n)‖ ≤ ‖u^n‖, and if Euler’s method solved backward in time in combination with the spatial discretization L̃ in (2.11) is also strongly stable under the CFL restriction (2.4), ‖u^n − ΔtL̃(u^n)‖ ≤ ‖u^n‖, then the multistep method (2.14) is SSP, ‖u^{n+1}‖ ≤ ‖u^n‖, under the CFL restriction (2.6), Δt ≤ cΔt_FE, c = min_i α_i/|β_i|, (2.15) provided β_iL(·) is replaced by β_iL̃(·) whenever β_i is negative.

scheme.definition: Explicit multistep method (2.14): u^{n+1} = Σ_{i=1}^m (α_i u^{n+1−i} + Δtβ_i L(u^{n+1−i})), α_i ≥ 0, Σ α_i = 1, with β_iL replaced by β_iL̃ for negative β_i.

hypotheses.hypothesis: forward Euler with L and backward-in-time Euler with L̃ strongly stable under Δt ≤ Δt_FE
α_i ≥ 0, Σ α_i = 1

justification: The convex-combination argument (p. 93) gives ‖u^{n+1}‖ ≤ max_{1≤i≤m} ‖u^{n+1−i}‖, not the stated ‖u^{n+1}‖ ≤ ‖u^n‖. Hand-checked counterexample satisfying every hypothesis: scheme 2 of Table 5.1 (p. 105; α = (3/4, 0, 1/4), β = (3/2, 0, 0), c = 1/2) on the scalar ODE L(u) = −u. Forward Euler is non-expansive for Δt ≤ Δt_FE = 2, and L̃(u) = u satisfies the backward-Euler condition (it is never used because all β ≥ 0). With Δt = cΔt_FE = 1, u^{n+1} = −(3/4)u^n + (1/4)u^{n−2}. Starting from exact values u^0 = 1, u^1 = e^{−1}, u^2 = e^{−2} ≈ 0.1353 gives u^3 ≈ 0.1485 > |u^2|. The conclusion holds in the max-over-previous-steps form, so the error is in the stated inequality, not in the method.

sentence: The maximum CFL restriction attainable for such methods is the one dictated by the forward Euler scheme, Δt ≤ Δt_FE; i.e., (2.6) holds with maximal CFL coefficient c = 1.

scheme.definition: The family of m-stage, mth-order SSP Runge–Kutta methods (2.9) with nonnegative coefficients α_{i,k} and β_{i,k}; CFL coefficient (2.10) c = min α_{i,k}/β_{i,k}.
scheme.location: Proposition 3.1 first sentence, p. 94; eqs. (2.9)–(2.10), p. 92

hypotheses.hypothesis: Consider the family of m-stage, mth-order SSP Runge–Kutta methods (2.9) with nonnegative coefficients α_{i,k} and β_{i,k}.
section 3 setting: L linear, L(u) = Lu

justification: With hypotheses: the proof (p. 94) uses the linear order conditions A_{m,m−1} = 1/m!, A_{m,m−2} = 1/(m−1)!, which every m-th order method must satisfy, and shows that α_{k,k−1}/β_{k,k−1} ≥ 1 for all k forces all these ratios to equal 1, so c ≤ 1. In the linear setting of section 3, c = 1 is attained for every m by Proposition 3.2 (p. 95). Alone: the upper bound c ≤ 1 holds for any L. But if 'mth-order' is read as order for nonlinear L, the family is empty for m = 4 (Proposition 4.2, p. 101), so 'attainable' fails there; whether the sentence claims attainment or only the bound depends on the reading.

sentence: The class of m-stage schemes given (recursively) by u^(i) = u^(i−1) + ΔtLu^(i−1), i = 1, ..., m−1, (3.1) u^(m) = Σ_{k=0}^{m−2} α_{m,k}u^(k) + α_{m,m−1}(u^(m−1) + ΔtLu^(m−1)), where α_{1,0} = 1 and α_{m,k} = (1/k)α_{m−1,k−1}, k = 1, ..., m−2, (3.2) α_{m,m−1} = 1/m!, α_{m,0} = 1 − Σ_{k=1}^{m−1} α_{m,k} is an mth-order linear Runge–Kutta method which is SSP with CFL coefficient c = 1, Δt ≤ Δt_FE.

scheme.definition: (3.1)–(3.2) as quoted in the sentence; L linear (L(u) = Lu); coefficients tabulated up to m = 8 in Table 3.1.

hypotheses.hypothesis: L linear (section 3 setting); forward Euler strongly stable under Δt ≤ Δt_FE

justification: With hypotheses: the proof (pp. 95–96) shows by induction that the coefficient of (ΔtL)^k is 1/k! for k = 0, ..., m, which is m-th order for linear L. It also shows all α_{m,j} ≥ 0, and since the β's are α_{m,m−1} or 1 in Euler substeps, every α/β ratio is 1, giving c = 1 by Lemma 2.1. Spot check m = 3: 1/3 + (1/2)(1+z) + (1/6)(1+z)^3 = 1 + z + z^2/2 + z^3/6, which is (3.4). Alone: the sentence itself says 'linear Runge–Kutta method', and SSP with c = 1 holds for any L (p. 96, which notes it is no longer m-th order for nonlinear L).

sentence: Then the fourth-order Runge–Kutta scheme (3.9)–(3.13) is stable under CFL condition Δt_n ≤ 2η(t_n), (3.15) and the following estimate holds: |u^n| ≤ e^{3Kt_n}|u^0|. (3.16)

hypotheses.hypothesis: Consider the coercive systems of ODEs (3.6)–(3.7), with Lipschitz continuous coefficients (3.14).
coercivity: η(t) := inf_{|u|=1} −Re⟨L(t)u,u⟩/|L(t)u|^2 > 0
Lipschitz regularity: ‖L(t) − L(s)‖ ≤ (K/η(t))|t − s|

justification: With hypotheses: the proof (pp. 99–100) freezes L at t_n, which gives |v^{n+1}| ≤ |u^n| via (3.5), and then bounds the differences k_i − j_i. In (3.28)–(3.29) it bounds ‖L(t_{n+1/2})‖ and ‖L(t_{n+1})‖ by 1/η(t_n), but (3.8) only gives ‖L(t)‖ ≤ 1/η(t) at the same t. This is justified if η is constant; for time-varying η the extra terms change the constant, so the stated estimate with exactly 3K is not proven by the text as written. Some bound of the form e^{CKt} seems plausible, but we did not check it. Alone: η and K are defined only through the hypotheses (coercivity, Lipschitz), so the sentence has no definite content without them.

sentence: If we require β_{i,k} ≥ 0, then an optimal second-order SSP Runge–Kutta method (2.9) is given by u^(1) = u^n + ΔtL(u^n), (4.1) u^{n+1} = (1/2)u^n + (1/2)u^(1) + (1/2)ΔtL(u^(1)), with a CFL coefficient c = 1 in (2.10).

hypotheses.hypothesis: m-stage, mth-order methods, here m = 2 (section 4.1 looks at m-stage, mth-order methods for m = 2, 3, 4)
β_{i,k} ≥ 0 (α_{i,k} ≥ 0 is part of (2.9)); nonlinear L

justification: With hypotheses: proved in Gottlieb–Shu 1998, Proposition 3.1 (proof p. 78 there): c > 1 is impossible for two-stage second order methods with nonnegative coefficients, and (4.1) attains c = 1. Also consistent with Proposition 3.1 here (p. 94). Alone: without the two-stage restriction, a three-stage second order method with nonnegative coefficients has c = 2. Hand-checked: u^(1) = u^n + (1/2)ΔtL(u^n), u^(2) = u^(1) + (1/2)ΔtL(u^(1)), u^{n+1} = (1/3)u^n + (2/3)u^(2) + (1/3)ΔtL(u^(2)); Butcher weights (1/3, 1/3, 1/3), nodes (0, 1/2, 1), all α/β = 2. So (4.1) is not optimal among all second-order SSP methods (2.9), even per function evaluation (2/3 > 1/2).

sentence: An optimal third-order SSP Runge–Kutta method (2.9) is given by u^(1) = u^n + ΔtL(u^n), u^(2) = (3/4)u^n + (1/4)u^(1) + (1/4)ΔtL(u^(1)), (4.2) u^{n+1} = (1/3)u^n + (2/3)u^(2) + (2/3)ΔtL(u^(2)), with a CFL coefficient c = 1 in (2.10).
