Essentially three-point scheme (admits viscosity form (5.1))
Semi-discrete; 'only if' for three-point schemes p = 1

justification: The entropy balance (5.7), p. 473 (Tadmor 1987b, Theorem 5.2) writes the entropy production as −(1/(4Δx))[⟨Δv_{ν−1/2}, D_{ν−1/2}Δv_{ν−1/2}⟩ + ⟨Δv_{ν+1/2}, D_{ν+1/2}Δv_{ν+1/2}⟩] with D = Q − Q*. That is ≤ 0 under (5.6). The converse for three-point schemes is proved in Tadmor (1987, Math. Comp. 49, Theorem 5.2(ii) with proof (5.15)-(5.18), pp. 100-101). The sentence states its own condition, so alone is TRUE.

sentence: The conservative scheme d/dt u_ν(t) = −(1/(2Δx_ν))[f(u_{ν+1}) − f(u_{ν−1})] + (1/(2Δx_ν))[Q_{ν+1/2}Δv_{ν+1/2} − Q_{ν−1/2}Δv_{ν−1/2}] (5.22) is entropy-stable if the eigenvalues of (the symmetric part of) its viscosity coefficient matrix, Re Q_{ν+1/2}, satisfy min_λ λ[Re Q_{ν+1/2}] ≥ C_{ν+1/2}·|Δv_{ν+1/2}|. (5.23)

scheme.definition: Scheme (5.22) as in the sentence (essentially three-point viscosity form in entropy variables). C_{ν+1/2} is the constant in the cubic bound |⟨Δv_{ν+1/2}, Q*_{ν+1/2}Δv_{ν+1/2}⟩| ≤ C_{ν+1/2}·|Δv_{ν+1/2}|^3 (5.21) for the entropy-conservative viscosity (5.5).

hypotheses.hypothesis: System (2.1) with convex entropy; entropy variables; semi-discrete
C_{ν+1/2} as in (5.21) (bound on the entropy-conservative viscosity, derived via the eigen-expansion (5.19)-(5.20))

justification: From (5.23), ⟨Δv, Q Δv⟩ = ⟨Δv, Re Q Δv⟩ ≥ C|Δv|^3 ≥ ⟨Δv, Q* Δv⟩ by (5.21), so (5.6) holds and Corollary 5.1 (p. 472) gives entropy stability. The source derives the theorem this way ('Comparison of this in light of Corollary 5.1', p. 475). The sentence contains its condition, so alone is TRUE.

sentence: The scheme is entropy-stable if the eigenvalues of its viscosity coefficient matrix λ(P_{ν+1/2}) satisfy min_λ λ[P_{ν+1/2}] ≥ γ_{ν+1/2}|Δu_{ν+1/2}|. (5.27)

hypotheses.hypothesis: Consider the conservative difference scheme (5.24) with numerical viscosity coefficient P_{ν+1/2}, which is essentially H-symmetric (5.25), (5.26).
γ_{ν+1/2} is a suitably large constant depending on (5.21), (5.25), (5.26) for which γ_{ν+1/2} ≥ K(C_{ν+1/2} + δ_{ν+1/2}) (5.28)
System with convex entropy; semi-discrete

justification: With hypotheses: the proof on p. 477 rewrites (5.24) as (5.22) with Q = PH and reduces to Theorem 5.3. It splits H^{−1/2}PH^{1/2} into the symmetric part H^{−1/2}(Re Q)H^{−1/2} plus a skew part of size O(Kδ|Δu|) by (5.25). Passing from the eigenvalue bound on the non-symmetric matrix to its symmetric part is stated without detail. Standard eigenvalue perturbation justifies it up to a dimension-dependent constant, which the phrase 'suitably large constant' γ absorbs. Alone (without H-symmetry (5.25)): the eigenvalues of a non-symmetric P need not control the symmetric part of PH, and the sentence alone does not fix γ. I found no counterexample in the sources, so alone is UNSURE.

sentence: The conservative Roe-type scheme (5.24), (5.33), (5.34) is entropy-stable, provided that its viscosity function p(·) satisfies p(ã_k) ≥ KC_{ν+1/2}·|Δu_{ν+1/2}|, ã_k := λ_k[Ã_{ν+1/2}]. (5.35)

scheme.definition: Scheme (5.24) with P_{ν+1/2} = p(Ã_{ν+1/2}) (5.33), p(Ã_{ν+1/2}) = R_{ν+1/2}·diag(p(ã_1), ..., p(ã_N))·R^{−1}_{ν+1/2} (5.34), where Ã_{ν+1/2} is a Lipschitz-continuous Roe matrix with Δf_{ν+1/2} = Ã_{ν+1/2}Δu_{ν+1/2} (5.30) and complete real eigensystem, taken as Ã_{ν+1/2} = B_{ν+1/2}·H^{−1}_{ν+1/2} (5.31) with cell averages B_{ν+1/2} = ∫_{−1/2}^{1/2} B(v_{ν+1/2}(ξ)) dξ, H_{ν+1/2} = ∫_{−1/2}^{1/2} H(v_{ν+1/2}(ξ)) dξ (5.32).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Roe matrix (5.31)-(5.32); with this choice P is H-symmetric so (5.25) holds with δ = 0
H bounds (5.26) with constant K; C_{ν+1/2} from (5.21)
Semi-discrete; system with convex entropy

justification: On p. 478 the source shows P = H^{1/2} p[H^{−1/2} B H^{−1/2}] H^{−1/2}, so P is H-symmetric and δ = 0 in (5.25). Then (5.35) gives min λ(P) ≥ KC|Δu|, which is (5.27)-(5.28) with γ = KC, and Theorem 5.4 applies. The sentence states its condition, and the remaining set-up is the scheme's own definition, so alone is TRUE.

sentence: The conservative Roe-type scheme (5.24), (5.33), (5.34) is entropy-stable if its viscosity function, p(·), satisfies p(ã_k) ≥ (1/6)[Δa_k(u_ν) + ε_k|ã_k| + (1 + |ã_k|/ε_k) Const |Δu_{ν+1/2}|^2]. (5.40)

scheme.definition: Roe-type scheme (5.24), (5.33), (5.34) as in Example 5.6 (P_{ν+1/2} = p(Ã_{ν+1/2}) via the spectral decomposition of the Roe matrix Ã_{ν+1/2}); Δa_k(u_ν) = λ_k(A(u_{ν+1})) − λ_k(A(u_ν)).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Here ε_k > 0 are arbitrary parameters at our disposal.
Eigensystem of the Roe matrix within O(|Δu|^2) of that of the mid-value Jacobian A(ξ = 0): |r̃_k − r_k(ξ=0)| + |ã_k − a_k(ξ=0)| ≤ Const|Δu_{ν+1/2}|^2 (5.39) / (A.4)
H bounds (5.26); semi-discrete; system with convex entropy

justification: The Appendix proves it, p. 512. Lemma A1 bounds ⟨Δv, QΔv⟩ from below by Σ[p(ã_k) − Const|Δv|^2]∫|⟨r_k(ξ), Δv⟩|^2 dξ. Lemma A2 bounds ⟨Δv, Q*Δv⟩ from above by the right side of (5.40) times the same integrals. Comparing the two and applying Corollary 5.1 gives (A.22) ≡ (5.40), with the Const terms absorbed. The Remark on p. 480 says the essential ingredient is (5.39), which for the averaged Roe matrix (5.31)-(5.32) is asserted on p. 479. Alone the sentence already contains the viscosity condition, so it is TRUE, provided (5.39) holds for the Roe matrix as the source states.

sentence: The conservative scheme d/dt u_ν(t) = −(1/Δx_ν)[g*_{ν+1/2} − g*_{ν−1/2}], with a numerical flux g*_{ν+1/2} given by g*_{ν+1/2} = Σ_{j=1}^N [ψ(v^{j+1}_{ν+1/2}) − ψ(v^j_{ν+1/2})]/⟨ℓ^j_{ν+1/2}, Δv_{ν+1/2}⟩ · ℓ^j_{ν+1/2}, (6.3) is an entropy-conservative approximation consistent with (2.5).

scheme.definition: As in the sentence; {r^j_{ν+1/2}} an arbitrary set of N linearly independent N-vectors, {ℓ^j_{ν+1/2}} the dual set ⟨ℓ^j, r^k⟩ = δ_jk; intermediate states v^1 = v_ν, v^{j+1} = v^j + ⟨ℓ^j, Δv_{ν+1/2}⟩ r^j (6.1), so v^{N+1} = v_{ν+1} (6.2); ψ the entropy flux potential.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Here, ψ is the entropy flux potential associated with the conserved entropy pair (U, F).
{r^j} linearly independent with dual {ℓ^j}; quantities in (6.3) well defined by (6.6)
System with convex entropy; entropy variables; semi-discrete

justification: The proof is on pp. 483-484. ⟨Δv, g*⟩ telescopes to ψ(v^{N+1}) − ψ(v^1) = Δψ, which is (3.11), so Theorem 3.1 gives entropy conservation. Consistency g*(v, v) = Σ⟨g(v), r^j⟩ℓ^j = g(v) follows from the equivalent form (6.6)-(6.7). The theorem's set-up is the scheme's own definition, so alone is TRUE.

scheme.definition: As in the sentence; u^j_{ν+1/2} := u(v^j_{ν+1/2}) along the path (6.1); v^{j+1/2}_{ν+1/2}(ξ) := ½(v^j + v^{j+1}) + ξ⟨ℓ^j, Δv_{ν+1/2}⟩ r^j, −½ ≤ ξ ≤ ½ (6.4), the straight subpath between consecutive intermediate states; B = g_v.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Given a complete path in phase space, {u^j_{ν+1/2} := u(v^j_{ν+1/2})}_{j=1}^{N+1}, associated with left and right orthogonal sets ⟨ℓ^j_{ν+1/2}, r^k_{ν+1/2}⟩ = δ_jk, where r^j_{ν+1/2} is in the direction of v^{j+1}_{ν+1/2} − v^j_{ν+1/2}.
System with convex entropy; semi-discrete

justification: The scheme is Theorem 6.1's entropy-conservative scheme, rewritten by integrating each subpath factor of (6.6) by parts (p. 484). That gives ½⟨f(u^j) + f(u^{j+1}), r^j⟩ − ∫ξ⟨r^j, B r^j⟩dξ ⟨ℓ^j, Δv⟩, and with −(1/Δx)[g*_{ν+1/2} − g*_{ν−1/2}] this yields (6.8) with Q^{j+1/2,*} = ∫2ξB. The display on p. 484 shows a '+' before the ξ-integral, but the sign in (6.8) is the one integration by parts gives. Entropy conservation is inherited from Theorem 6.1. The sentence's hypotheses are only the definitions, so alone is TRUE.

sentence: The semi-discrete scheme d/dt u_ν(t) = −(1/(2Δx_ν))[Σ_{j=1}^N ⟨f(u^j_{ν+1/2}) + f(u^{j+1}_{ν+1/2}), r^j_{ν+1/2}⟩ℓ^j_{ν+1/2} − ⟨f(u^j_{ν−1/2}) + f(u^{j+1}_{ν−1/2}), r^j_{ν−1/2}⟩ℓ^j_{ν−1/2}] + (1/(2Δx_ν))[Σ_{j=1}^N q^{j+1/2}_{ν+1/2}⟨ℓ^j_{ν+1/2}, Δv_{ν+1/2}⟩ℓ^j_{ν+1/2} − Σ_{j=1}^N q^{j+1/2}_{ν−1/2}⟨ℓ^j_{ν−1/2}, Δv_{ν−1/2}⟩ℓ^j_{ν−1/2}], (6.10) is entropy-stable if it contains more numerical viscosity than the entropy-conservative one in the sense that (6.9) holds.

scheme.definition: As in the sentence (6.10), with viscosity amplitudes q^{j+1/2}_{ν+1/2} along each subpath of the path (6.1); comparison condition (6.9): ⟨r^j_{ν+1/2}, Q^{j+1/2,*}_{ν+1/2} r^j_{ν+1/2}⟩ ≤ q^{j+1/2}_{ν+1/2}, with Q^{j+1/2,*} from (6.8).

hypotheses.hypothesis: (6.9) holds for every j and every cell
Path and dual bases as in Corollary 6.2; system with convex entropy; semi-discrete

justification: The source gives no written proof ('A straightforward argument along the lines of our previous results', p. 485), but the argument is direct. The flux of (6.10) equals g* − ½Σ_j (q^j − ⟨r^j, Q^{j,*} r^j⟩)⟨ℓ^j, Δv⟩ℓ^j, with g* from Corollary 6.2. So ⟨Δv, g⟩ − Δψ = −½Σ_j (q^j − ⟨r^j, Q^{j,*} r^j⟩)⟨ℓ^j, Δv⟩^2 ≤ 0 under (6.9), and Theorem 3.1 (3.10) gives entropy stability. The sentence contains its own condition, so alone is TRUE.

sentence: The difference scheme (6.10), (6.12) is a second-order accurate entropy-stable approximation of (2.1).

scheme.definition: Scheme (6.10) with viscosity amplitude along the j-wave q^{j+1/2}_{ν+1/2} = ∫_{−1/2}^{1/2} (¼ − ξ^2) ⟨∇_u a_j(u^{j+1/2}_{ν+1/2}(ξ)), r^j_{ν+1/2}⟩^+ dξ (6.12), path breakpoints u^j_{ν+1/2} along the (approximate) Riemann solution, w_k ∼ r^k the normalized eigensystem of A.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Symmetric case where entropy and conservative variables coincide, B(v) = A(u)
Subpaths chosen along the eigensystem of A at the Riemann-solution breakpoints (Lax 1957), so all but one term of (6.11) vanish to higher order in |Δu|

justification: Entropy stability needs (6.9), q ≥ ⟨r^j, Q^{j,*} r^j⟩ (Theorem 6.3). But (6.12) only matches the leading term of the expansion (6.11), written with '≈' on p. 487, and the neglected higher-order terms in |Δu| are not bounded. The analysis covers only the symmetric case B = A, and the general case is left as 'lengthy calculations' (p. 487). No proof is given ('We conclude this section with the following two corollaries', p. 488). Second-order accuracy is plausible because q = O(|Δv|) (Lemma 4.5), but the entropy-stability part is not established in the source.

sentence: No artificial dissipation is added in shocks and, in particular, it has the desirable property of keeping the sharpness of shock profiles.

scheme.definition: Scheme (6.10), (6.12) as in tadmor_2003_acta:15.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Symmetric case B(v) = A(u); path along the (approximate) Riemann solution

justification: On p. 487 the source identifies j-shocks with ⟨∇_u a_j, r^j⟩ > 0, where the entropy-conservative viscosity is positive. There (6.12) keeps exactly the leading term, adding nothing beyond the entropy-conservative viscosity, and the positive part only removes the anti-diffusion on rarefactions. So the first clause holds by construction to leading order. 'Keeping the sharpness of shock profiles' is qualitative, and the source gives no proof or computation for it. Entropy-conservative schemes are themselves the zero-dispersion reference (Example 4.2, p. 466), so sharp shock profiles do not follow from the construction. UNSURE both ways.

sentence: The following Lax–Wendroff-type difference scheme is a second-order accurate entropy-stable approximation of (2.1): d/dt u_ν(t) = −(1/(2Δx_ν))[Σ_{j=1}^N ⟨f(u^j_{ν+1/2}) + f(u^{j+1}_{ν+1/2}), r^j_{ν+1/2}⟩ℓ^j_{ν+1/2} − ⟨f(u^j_{ν−1/2}) + f(u^{j+1}_{ν−1/2}), r^j_{ν−1/2}⟩ℓ^j_{ν−1/2}] + (1/(8Δx_ν))[Σ_{j=1}^N [a_j(u^{j+1}_{ν+1/2}) − a_j(u^j_{ν+1/2})]^+ ℓ^j_{ν+1/2} − Σ_{j=1}^N [a_j(u^{j+1}_{ν−1/2}) − a_j(u^j_{ν−1/2})]^+ ℓ^j_{ν−1/2}]. (6.14)

scheme.definition: As in the sentence (6.14); obtained from (6.10), (6.12) via the upper bound ∫(¼ − ξ^2)⟨∇_u a_j(u(ξ)), r^j⟩^+ dξ ≤ ¼[a_j(u^{j+1}_{ν+1/2}) − a_j(u^j_{ν+1/2})]^+ ⟨ℓ^j_{ν+1/2}, Δv_{ν+1/2}⟩ (6.13) (as printed).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Path connecting u^j and u^{j+1} chosen along the (approximate) Riemann solution, so the integrand of (6.12) does not change sign
Symmetric case B = A as in the derivation of (6.12)

justification: The scheme replaces q in (6.12) by the upper bound (6.13), so its entropy stability rests on Corollary 6.4. That corollary is only a leading-order argument in the symmetric case with no proof (see tadmor_2003_acta:15). The bound (6.13) is said to follow 'along the lines of Example 4.7' without detail, and as printed the viscosity term in (6.14) lacks the ⟨ℓ^j, Δv⟩ factor that appears in (6.13). The source does not settle entropy stability, so UNSURE both ways.

sentence: No artificial dissipation is added in shocks and in particular, it has the desirable property of keeping the sharpness of shock profiles.

scheme.definition: Lax–Wendroff-type scheme (6.14), as in tadmor_2003_acta:17.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Path along the (approximate) Riemann solution; symmetric case

justification: In (6.14) the viscosity on a j-shock is the upper bound ¼[Δa_j]^+ from (6.13), not the entropy-conservative amount ∫(¼ − ξ^2)⟨∇a_j, r^j⟩dξ. For a linear variation of a_j along the subpath, that amount is Δa_j/6 < Δa_j/4. So some dissipation beyond the entropy-conservative reference is added in shocks, and 'no artificial dissipation' holds at best in a loose sense. Shock sharpness is not demonstrated in the source. I treat the sentence as part of the corollary statement because the source tadmor_2003_acta layer sets it in the same style as the statement.

sentence: The Crank–Nicolson scheme (7.22), (7.23) is entropy-stable (and, respectively, entropy-conservative), if and only if the semi-discrete scheme associated with the numerical flux g(·) is entropy-stable (respectively, entropy-conservative).

scheme.definition: v^{n+1/2} := ∫_{−1/2}^{1/2} v(½(u^n + u^{n+1}) + ξΔu^{n+1/2}) dξ, Δu^{n+1/2} = u^{n+1} − u^n (7.22); u^{n+1}_ν = u^n_ν − (Δt/Δx)[g_{ν+1/2}(v^{n+1/2}) − g_{ν−1/2}(v^{n+1/2})] (7.23), where g is the essentially three-point numerical flux of the semi-discrete scheme (7.1)-(7.2).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Entropy-weighted mid-value (7.22) (not the arithmetic mean, except in the symmetric case)
System with convex entropy; implicit system (7.23) solvable

justification: The proof is the one-line identity ⟨v^{n+1/2}, u^{n+1} − u^n⟩ = U(u^{n+1}) − U(u^n), p. 494, which holds because ∫⟨v(u(ξ)), Δu⟩dξ = ∫dU along the straight path. So U(u^{n+1}_ν) − U(u^n_ν) = −(Δt/Δx)⟨v^{n+1/2}_ν, g_{ν+1/2} − g_{ν−1/2}⟩ evaluated at v^{n+1/2}. The fully discrete entropy balance is therefore exactly Δt times the semi-discrete one at the state v^{n+1/2}, giving 'if'. 'Only if' needs every grid state to arise as some v^{n+1/2}, which the source does not discuss but which holds generically for small Δt. The sentence states its own condition; alone TRUE.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Consider the fully discrete scalar scheme (8.1) and assume the CFL condition (Δt/Δx)|a(u^n_{ν+1/2}(s))| ≤ (Δt/Δx)p_{ν+1/2} ≤ I − (Δt/Δx)|a(u^n_{ν+1/2}(r, s))| (8.8) is fulfilled. (I printed for the scalar 1.)
Any convex entropy pair (U, F) of the scalar law; a = f'

justification: With hypotheses: the homotopy computation (8.2)-(8.7), pp. 494-496, shows I_+ ≤ 0 and I_− ≤ 0 under (8.6) and its mirror, which combine into (8.8). Convexity gives the first inequality, and averaging I_± gives the second. Caveat: averaging gives −(Δt/(2Δx))[F(u^n_{ν+1}) − F(u^n_{ν−1})], as in Corollary 8.2. The printed factor Δt/Δx (both text layers) is a misprint, and with it the displayed inequality would fail for smooth data. TRUE refers to the derived inequality. Alone (no CFL): FALSE. With U = u^2/2 and summing over ν, the inequality implies ℓ2 non-increase, which fails for the linear modified Lax–Friedrichs case at large Δt/Δx. Its von Neumann amplification factor exceeds 1 there (my computation), and the source says the CFL condition is sharp (p. 498). Policy: sentences are judged as printed. As printed (factor Δt/Δx in front of the entropy-flux difference instead of Δt/(2Δx)), the inequality fails for smooth data with F(u_{ν+1}) − F(u_{ν−1}) of order Δx, so expected_with_hypotheses is FALSE; the inequality the proof derives (with Δt/(2Δx)) is TRUE under the CFL condition.

sentence: Then the following cell entropy inequality holds for the quadratic entropy pair U(u) = |u|^2/2, F(u) = ∫^u f(w)dw − ⟨u, f(u)⟩: U(u^{n+1}_ν) ≤ ½(U(u^{n+1}_{ν+1/2}) + U(u^{n+1}_{ν−1/2})) ≤ U(u^n_ν) − (Δt/(2Δx))(F(u^n_{ν+1}) − F(u^n_{ν−1})) + (Δt/(2Δx))(∫_0^1 ⟨U'(v^n_{ν+1/2}(s)), P_{ν+1/2}(u^n_{ν+1} − u^n_ν)⟩ ds − ∫_0^1 ⟨U'(u^n_{ν−1/2}(s)), P_{ν−1/2}(u^n_ν − u^n_{ν−1})⟩ ds).

scheme.definition: Fully discrete scheme (8.1) for a symmetric system, u^{n+1}_ν = u^n_ν − (Δt/(2Δx))[f(u^n_{ν+1}) − f(u^n_{ν−1})] + (Δt/(2Δx))[P_{ν+1/2}(u^n_{ν+1} − u^n_ν) − P_{ν−1/2}(u^n_ν − u^n_{ν−1})], with the left/right decomposition and homotopy variables (8.4) as in Corollary 8.1; |A| defined by spectral decomposition (footnote 5).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Consider the fully discrete scheme (8.1) consistent with the symmetric system (2.1) and assume the CFL condition (Δt/Δx)|A(u^n_{ν+1/2}(s))| ≤ (Δt/Δx)P_{ν+1/2} ≤ I − (Δt/Δx)|A(u^n_{ν+1/2}(r, s))| (8.10) is fulfilled.
Symmetric system (A = f_u symmetric), quadratic entropy only; C(s) = P − A(u(s)) symmetric

justification: With hypotheses: (8.9), p. 497, writes I_+ as a double integral of ⟨(I − (Δt/Δx)C(t))Δu, (Δt/Δx)C(s)Δu⟩. It is nonnegative when 0 ≤ C and (Δt/Δx)λ(C) ≤ 1 (via Sylvester's theorem), which (8.10) gives. Averaging the two halves gives the inequality. Caveat: the printed entropy flux has the wrong sign (the flux of U = |u|^2/2 is ⟨u, f(u)⟩ − ∫^u f, whose derivative is u^T A), and 'U'(v^n_{ν+1/2}(s))' should read u. TRUE refers to the inequality as derived. Alone (no CFL): FALSE, by the same ℓ2/von Neumann argument as tadmor_2003_acta:20 (source: CFL sharp, p. 498). Policy: sentences are judged as printed. As printed, F(u) = ∫^u f − ⟨u, f(u)⟩ is minus the entropy flux of U = |u|^2/2 (its gradient is −u^T A instead of u^T A), so the printed inequality is false for smooth data and expected_with_hypotheses is FALSE; with the correct flux ⟨u, f(u)⟩ − ∫^u f the derived inequality is TRUE under (8.10).

sentence: The resulting five-point scheme (9.5), (9.6), (9.7) is entropy-conservative, and it is of (at least) third-order accuracy provided Q**(v, v, v) = B(v).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Q**(v, v, v) = B(v) (for the accuracy part)
System with convex entropy; entropy variables; semi-discrete

justification: Stated without proof and attributed to LeFloch and Rohde (2000, Section 3), which I did not read. The source's own derivation (pp. 500-501) only motivates higher-order entropy-conservative schemes via piecewise polynomial finite elements. Entropy conservation of the five-point flux needs a modified wide-stencil entropy flux that is not shown here, and the third-order truncation error is not computed. Nothing I read settles it.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Let {r̃_k, ã_k} be the eigensystem of Ã_{ν+1/2}, and assume that |r̃_k − r_k(ξ=0)| + |ã_k − a_k(ξ=0)| ≤ Const|Δv_{ν+1/2}|^2. (A.4)
H(ξ) ≤ K·I_N (5.26); orthonormal system {H^{−1/2}(ξ) r_k(ξ)} (5.18)

Expand in the orthonormal system (5.18), Taylor-expand r_k(ξ) using (A.4) and (A.7) to get (A.8), bound the remainder terms II, III by Const|Δv|^4 ((A.11)-(A.12)), and convert with (A.13). Alone (without the eigensystem-closeness assumption (A.4) and with 'Const' unspecified), the bound is not established. For the averaged Roe matrix (5.31)-(5.32) the source asserts (5.39) on p. 479, but it does not prove it, so alone is UNSURE.

scheme.definition: Entropy-conservative scheme (5.2), (5.3) (straight-path flux g*_{ν+1/2} = ∫_{−1/2}^{1/2} g(v_{ν+1/2}(ξ)) dξ) with viscosity matrix Q*_{ν+1/2} = ∫_{−1/2}^{1/2} 2ξB(v_{ν+1/2}(ξ)) dξ (5.5); Δa_k(u_ν) ≡ a_k(u_{ν+1}) − a_k(u_ν), a_k = λ_k(A(u)).

Roe-matrix eigensystem closeness (A.4) (used in the proof to replace a_k(0) by ã_k); H bounds (5.26)

justification: With hypotheses: proved on pp. 510-512, via the eigen-expansion (5.19), symmetrization ξ → −ξ (A.15), Taylor expansions (A.16)-(A.18), Cauchy–Schwarz with ε_k (A.20), (A.13), and ȧ_k(0) = Δa_k(u_ν) + O(|Δv|^2). The proof uses (A.4) to pass from a_k(0) to ã_k, which the lemma statement does not list, so alone (without (A.4)) is UNSURE.

sentence: We present an hierarchy of uniformly high order accurate schemes which generalizes Godunov's scheme and its second order accurate MUSCL extension to arbitrary order of accuracy.

scheme.definition: ENO schemes (1.10) Ē_h(τ)w̄ = A_h·E(τ)·R(·; w̄), carried out as (1.14): (i) reconstruction v_h(x, t_n + 0) = R(x; v^n), a piecewise polynomial of degree r - 1 with R(x; w̄) = w(x) + e(x)h^r + O(h^{r+1}) where w is smooth (1.9a), conservation of cell averages (1.9b), and TV(R) ≤ TV(w) + O(h^r) (1.9c); (ii) exact (or approximate) solution in the small v_h(·, t) = E(t - t_n)v_h(·, t_n + 0); (iii) cell averaging v_j^{n+1} = cell average of v_h(·, t_{n+1} - 0). Equivalent conservation form v_j^{n+1} = v_j^n - λ(f̄_{j+1/2} - f̄_{j-1/2}) with f̄_{j+1/2} = (1/τ)∫_0^τ f(v_h(x_{j+1/2}, t_n + η)) dη (1.16). R is built by ENO interpolation via the primitive function (RP, (3.8)) or by deconvolution (RD, (3.18)); r = 1 gives Godunov's scheme (1.11), r = 2 the MUSCL-type schemes (1.12).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Accuracy is in the sense of local truncation error of cell averages, O(h^{r+1}) away from discontinuities and points where e(x) fails to be Lipschitz continuous (1.8b), (1.17c).
u smooth and the numerical approximation assumed to converge; then 'we expect the cumulative error to be O(h^r)' (1.18a).

Where e(x) is not Lipschitz (local extrema for MUSCL-type schemes, roots of higher derivatives for higher order) the pointwise error is only O(h^{r-1}); '"r-th order accurate"' in quotes means r-th order in L1 but (r - 1)-th in the maximum norm; RP with m = r and RD with m = r - 1 are of this kind, RD with m = r is r-th order pointwise.
hypotheses.location: Remark (1.2), printed pp. 8-9; Remark (3.1), printed p. 23

hypotheses.hypothesis: h small enough that at least r + 1 points of smoothness separate discontinuities.

justification: Shu, 'Numerical experiments on the accuracy of ENO and modified ENO schemes', ICASE Report 90-55 (NASA CR-182083), 1990 (shu90, pp. 1-3, Figs. 2a, 4a, 4b; Concluding Remarks p. 6), following Rogerson and Meiburg: for u_t + u_x = 0 with smooth periodic data u0 = sin^4(πx), third-order ENO converges in L1 at about 1.97 (TVD Runge-Kutta) and about 2.5 even with exact time evolution, with the same behaviour for 'the original cell-averaged ENO schemes in [3]' ([3] is the journal version of this paper); 'ENO schemes may lose the full high order accuracy predicted by local truncation error analysis'. This case meets every hypothesis the paper states (smooth solution, linear problem), so even the L1 sense of Remark (1.2) fails; only the formal local truncation error claim (pp. 7-8) survives, and the O(h^r) cumulative error is only 'expected' (p. 8). Alone it is FALSE for the same reason, and also because the paper itself says some versions are only (r - 1)-th order in the maximum norm (pp. 8-9, 23). The side claim that MUSCL is second order holds only in the L1 sense: the paper puts it in quotes and notes the loss at extrema (printed pp. 11, 24). This verdict rests on numerical evidence, not a proof.

sentence: The reconstruction algorithm is derived from a new interpolation technique that when applied to piecewise smooth data gives high-order accuracy whenever the function is smooth but avoids a Gibbs phenomenon at discontinuities.

scheme.definition: ENO interpolation H_m(x; w): H_m(x_j; w) = w(x_j) (3.1a), H_m = q_{m,j+1/2} on [x_j, x_{j+1}] (3.1b), q_{m,j+1/2} the m-th degree polynomial interpolating w at x_i, i_m(j) ≤ i ≤ i_m(j) + m, with 1 - m ≤ i_m(j) - j ≤ 0 (3.2); the stencil grows from i_1(j) = j (3.4a) by adding the left or right neighbour, whichever gives the (k+1)-th divided difference smaller in absolute value (3.4b). Used for reconstruction via the primitive function (3.6)-(3.8) or via deconvolution (3.11)-(3.18).

hypotheses.hypothesis: (3.5a) derivatives of H_m approximate those of w to O(h^{m+1-k}) wherever w is smooth; (3.5b) TV(H_m(·; w)) ≤ TV(w) + O(h^{m+1}). Shown in [16], not in this paper.
Avoiding a Gibbs phenomenon means no O(1) spurious oscillations proportional to the jump; O(h^r) oscillations may still occur in smooth parts.

For h sufficiently small, at least r + 1 points of smoothness separate discontinuities; when discontinuities are about to collide there are not enough points and large spurious oscillations may occur (system case).

justification: The paper only quotes (3.5a)-(3.5b) from its companion paper [16] ('In [16] we analyse this interpolation technique ... and show that', p. 18) and gives no proof here; we have not read [16]. Shu 1990 (shu90) concerns the time-dependent schemes, not the interpolation. Alone, the sentence omits the separation assumption that the paper says is needed for the non-oscillation bound (pp. 10, 14), but for a fixed piecewise smooth function it holds once h is small, so we cannot call it false. UNSURE both ways.

sentence: Unlike standard finite difference methods this procedure uses an adaptive stencil of grid points and consequently the resulting schemes are highly nonlinear.

scheme.definition: ENO schemes (1.10)/(1.14) with reconstruction from the adaptive-stencil ENO interpolation (3.1)-(3.4) (stencil chosen by comparing absolute values of divided differences of the data, (3.4b)); the RD variant also uses the min mod function (3.16).

justification: The stencil choice (3.4b) depends on the magnitudes of divided differences of the data, so the update is not a linear function of the data even for the linear equation u_t + a u_x = 0; the paper states this on printed p. 12 ('Due to the adaptive selection of stencil in the reconstruction step, the scheme ... is highly nonlinear; consequently the use of the standard linear stability analysis is inappropriate'), and Shu 1990 (shu90, p. 1) refers to 'the nonlinearity of the scheme'. 'highly' adds no checkable condition; read as 'nonlinear, even for linear problems', TRUE both ways.

sentence: The existence of a cell entropy inequality is discussed and such an equality for all entropies is shown to imply that the scheme is an E scheme on monotone (actually more general) data, hence at most only first order accurate in general.

scheme.definition: Two-level explicit scheme (1.1) v_v(t+k) = H(v_{v-p},...,v_{v+p}; f, λ), λ = k/Δx, for u_t + f(u)_x = 0 (1.2), assumed (Assumption 1.1) to have (i) Lax-Wendroff conservative form (1.3) with a Lipschitz continuous numerical flux h_{v+1/2} = h(v_{v-p+1},...,v_{v+p}; f, λ) consistent with f, h(w,...,w; f, λ) = f(w), and (ii) incremental form (1.4) H = v_v + C^+_{v+1/2} Δv_{v+1/2} - C^-_{v-1/2} Δv_{v-1/2}. For the necessity result (Theorem 7.3) the scheme is replaced by its semi-discrete limit dv_v/dt + (h_{v+1/2} - h_{v-1/2})/Δx = 0 (7.11a), with h allowed to depend on Δx (7.11b). E-flux: condition (i) on p. 45, s^+_{v+1/2}·[h_{v+1/2} - f(v)] ≤ 0 for v between the grid values (partly illegible in scan); p. 45 says the corresponding schemes are 'exactly those having more numerical viscosity than that of Godunov's scheme'.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The cell entropy inequality (7.12a) holds for all consistent numerical entropy pairs (U,F) (7.12b).
Semi-discrete approximation (7.11), obtained from (1.1) by the limit Δt → 0.
The conclusion is for separating intervals (7.13) of separated data; a monotone profile is the canonical example.
First-order limitation: the E-condition keeps the modified numerical viscosity away from that of Lax-Wendroff, so (3.4) fails; 'The proof follows along the lines of [18]'.

justification: With hypotheses: Theorem 7.3 (p. 50; proof pp. 50-51 with Kruzkov's entropies U(w) = |w - v|) proves that if the semi-discrete scheme (7.11) satisfies the cell entropy inequality for all consistent entropy pairs, its flux is an E-flux in every separating interval (monotone data, p. 49). The first-order part is argued on p. 51 (the E-condition bounds the viscosity away from Lax-Wendroff's, so the second-order requirement (3.4) fails, 'along the lines of [18]'); Tadmor, Acta Numerica 2003 (tad03, p. 468) also states 'The E-schemes are only first-order accurate'. Alone: the sentence speaks of 'the scheme', i.e. the fully discrete two-level scheme (1.1), but necessity is proved only for the semi-discrete limit (7.11) (p. 48: 'take the limit Δt → 0'); nothing we read settles the fully discrete case, so UNSURE. 'equality' is verbatim in both extractions (the context is the cell entropy inequality).

sentence: Convergence for TVD-SOR schemes approximating convex or concave conservation laws is shown by enforcing a single discrete entropy inequality.

scheme.definition: SOR-TVD schemes of Section 8: the piecewise constant viscosity modification of Theorem 4.7 applied to a 3-point upwind E-type scheme, with Q^SOR_{v+1/2} = Q_{v+1/2}(f) + Δg_{v+1/2}/Δv_{v+1/2} (8.1b), flux correction (8.1c), the choice of λ^2(a^2)_{v+1/2} in (8.9) / (8.13) involving Max|f''| over I_{v+1/2}, numerical flux modification h_{v+1/2} = ½[g_v + g_{v+1} - s_{v+1/2}|g_{v+1} - g_v|] (8.10b) and scheme (8.10c) (most displays illegible in scan). Single entropy pair U(v) = v^2/2, F(v) = ∫^v w f'(w) dw (p. 52).

hypotheses.hypothesis: f strictly convex ('the genuinely nonlinear case where f is, say, strictly convex').
Q_{v+1/2}(f) is an upwind E-type viscosity.
CFL condition λ·Max|f'(v)| ≤ 1/3 (8.11).
The step from TVD plus the single quadratic entropy inequality to convergence uses [14,5] (Lax; DiPerna).

justification: With hypotheses: Theorem 8.5 (p. 61) states TVD, second-order resolution, a quadratic cell entropy inequality and, as a consequence, convergence to the unique physically relevant solution, for strictly convex f, an upwind E-type base viscosity and λ max|f'| ≤ 1/3; the proof is Section 8 (Lemma 8.1, Proposition 8.2 with proof pp. 62-65, Lemma 8.3, Theorem 8.4), and the convergence step cites [14,5] (p. 52). Alone: the abstract says 'convex or concave' while the theorem needs strict convexity, and it drops the CFL bound 1/3 and the upwind E-type base; the concave case is not proved separately. Nothing we read says whether one entropy inequality suffices for convex but not strictly convex fluxes, so UNSURE.

sentence: The difference scheme (4.3), (4.14) is SOR-TVD under the CFL-like condition (4.15)

scheme.definition: Scheme (4.3) (flux correction g_v = s_v·Min(...) and modified flux, see Theorem 4.3) with the piecewise constant viscosity modification (4.14), Q^SOR_{v+1/2} = Q_{v+1/2}(f) + Δg_{v+1/2}/Δv_{v+1/2} (as restated in (8.1b), p. 52; (4.14) itself partly illegible in scan).

hypotheses.hypothesis: CFL-like condition (4.15): illegible in scan (a bound on the 3-point viscosity; Remark 4.8 says it can be improved to (4.12)).
The underlying 3-point scheme satisfies (4.1).

justification: With hypotheses: proof p. 22: SOR (4.4b) holds by the definition (4.14), the left TVD inequality follows from (4.1), and the right one, Q^SOR ≤ 1 (4.17), follows from the pessimistic bound (4.18) and (4.15). SOR is formal second order except at nonsonic critical values (p. 13). Alone: the CFL-like condition is part of the sentence, so TRUE.

location: p. 50, Theorem 7.3 (E-flux is necessary for cell entropy inequality)
sentence: Then the numerical flux, h, is an E-flux in any separating interval.

scheme.definition: Semi-discrete approximation dv_v/dt + (h_{v+1/2} - h_{v-1/2})/Δx = 0 (7.11a) with numerical flux h_{v+1/2} = h(v_{v-p+1},...,v_{v+p}; f, λ → 0, Δx) (7.11b). E-flux: condition (i), p. 45.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The cell entropy inequality (7.12a) holds for all consistent numerical entropy pairs (U, F) (7.12b).
Separating interval: all grid values in the stencil lie on one side or the other of I_{j+1/2} (7.13); monotone data are separated.

justification: With hypotheses: proved on pp. 50-51 from the entropy equality (7.14) with Kruzkov's entropies U(w) = |w - v|, the extension (7.16b) and the telescoping inequalities (7.17)-(7.18). TRUE. Alone (without the hypothesis that all entropy inequalities hold) the claim would make every consistent flux an E-flux, which fails: the central flux h = (f(v_j) + f(v_{j+1}))/2 for f = u^2/2 with v_j = 0, v_{j+1} = 1 (monotone, hence separated) gives h = 1/4 > f(0.1) = 0.005 although v_{j+1} > v_j, violating condition (i) on p. 45. FALSE.

sentence: This paper presents a class of new explicit second order accurate finite difference schemes for the computation of weak solutions of hyperbolic conservation laws.

scheme.definition: Scalar: a 3-point first order TVNI scheme with numerical flux f_{j+1/2} = ½[f(v_j) + f(v_{j+1}) - (1/λ) Q(ν_{j+1/2}) Δ_{j+1/2}v] (3.1a), ν = λ ā_{j+1/2}, ā_{j+1/2} = [f(v_{j+1}) - f(v_j)]/Δ_{j+1/2}v (3.1b), applied to the modified flux values f(v_i) + (1/λ) g_i (3.8a), giving the 5-point flux ½[f(v_j) + f(v_{j+1}) + (1/λ)(g_j + g_{j+1} - Q(ν_{j+1/2} + γ_{j+1/2}) Δ_{j+1/2}v)] (3.8d), γ_{j+1/2} = (g_{j+1} - g_j)/Δ_{j+1/2}v (3.8c), with g_i = s_{i+1/2} max[0, min(|g̃_{i+1/2}|, g̃_{i-1/2} s_{i+1/2})] (3.11a), g̃_{i+1/2} = ½[Q(ν_{i+1/2}) - (ν_{i+1/2})^2] Δ_{i+1/2}v (3.11b), s_{i+1/2} = sign(g̃_{i+1/2}) (3.11c). Systems: the field-by-field extension (4.8) using Roe-type averaged eigenvectors. Formulas partly garbled in the scan.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Second order in the sense of the flux condition (3.6), f̃_{j+1/2} - f^{LW}_{j+1/2} = O(Δ^2) for smooth solutions; (3.6) 'is only a necessary condition for second order accuracy', sufficient if the O(Δ^2) coefficient is differentiable except at finitely many points.
The scheme 'may degenerate locally to O(Δ^2) truncation error' where s_{j+1/2} is discontinuous, i.e. where Q(ν) - ν^2 = 0 or u_x = 0; 'truncation error ... O(Δ^3), except possibly where u_x = 0'.
Q Lipschitz continuous.

justification: With hypotheses: Lemmas 3.2-3.3 (pp. 15-18) prove the second-order flux condition (3.6) for smooth solutions (Lemma 4.1, p. 25, for systems), and Remark (2), p. 20 and p. 32 limit the claim to points away from u_x = 0 (and Q(ν) = ν^2); in that formal truncation-error sense TRUE. Alone: read as second order everywhere for smooth solutions it fails: the source itself says the scheme may degenerate to O(Δ^2) local truncation error at extrema (p. 20), and Osher-Tadmor 1985 (ot85, pp. 13, 15) show that a TVD scheme must give up second-order accuracy at nonsonic critical values. FALSE.

sentence: (i) A monotone scheme is TVNI.

scheme.definition: Explicit (2k+1)-point scheme in conservation form v_j^{n+1} = H(v_{j-k},...,v_{j+k}) = v_j - λ[f(v_{j-k+1},...,v_{j+k}) - f(v_{j-k},...,v_{j+k-1})] (2.3a) with consistent numerical flux (1.4c); monotone: H is a monotone nondecreasing function of each of its 2k+1 arguments; TVNI: TV(L·v) ≤ TV(v) for all v of bounded total variation (2.4).

justification: Proof p. 7: monotone schemes (in conservation form) form an L1-contractive semigroup (Keyfitz, cited as [8]), and applying the contraction to v and its translate z_j = v_{j+1} gives TV(L·v) ≤ TV(v). The sentence needs no hypotheses beyond the definitions on p. 6, so TRUE both alone and with hypotheses.

sentence: (ii) A TVNI scheme is monotonicity preserving.

scheme.definition: Explicit (2k+1)-point scheme in conservation form (2.3); TVNI as in (2.4); monotonicity preserving: if v is a monotone mesh function so is L·v.

justification: Proof p. 7: by finite support it suffices to take monotone v that is constant v_L to the left and v_R to the right; if w = L·v were not monotone it would have a local minimum and maximum, giving TV(w) ≥ |v_R - v_L| + |v_m - v_M| > TV(v), contradicting TVNI. No further hypotheses are needed, so TRUE both ways.

sentence: Let the coefficients C in (2.9c) satisfy the inequalities C_{-,j+1/2} ≥ 0, C_{+,j+1/2} ≥ 0 (2.10a) C_{-,j+1/2} + C_{+,j+1/2} ≤ 1 (2.10b) then the scheme (2.9) is TVNI.
justification: Proof p. 10: differencing (2.9b) gives (2.11) with coefficients C_{-,i-1/2}, 1 - C_{-,i+1/2} - C_{+,i+1/2}, C_{+,i+3/2}, all nonnegative by (2.10); taking absolute values and summing over i yields TV(w) ≤ TV(v). The hypotheses are in the sentence, so TRUE alone as well.

sentence: Let Q(x) in (3.1a) satisfy the inequalities |x| ≤ Q(x) ≤ 1 for 0 ≤ |x| ≤ μ, (3.2) then the finite-difference scheme (1.4) with (3.1) is TVNI under the CFL-like restriction λ max_j |ā_{j+1/2}| ≤ μ (3.3)

scheme.definition: 3-point conservative scheme (1.4) with numerical flux f_{j+1/2} = ½[f(v_j) + f(v_{j+1}) - (1/λ) Q(λ ā_{j+1/2}) Δ_{j+1/2}v] (3.1a), ā_{j+1/2} = [f(v_{j+1}) - f(v_j)]/Δ_{j+1/2}v if Δ_{j+1/2}v ≠ 0, a(v_j) otherwise (3.1b); Q is the coefficient of numerical viscosity.

justification: Proof pp. 12-13: the scheme is rewritten in the form (2.9) with C± = ½[Q(ν_{j+1/2}) ∓ ν_{j+1/2}] (3.5), so C± ≥ 0 and C+ + C- = Q(ν) ≤ 1 under (3.2)-(3.3), and Lemma 2.2 applies. The reading of (3.2)-(3.3) is supported by p. 32 ('it is the requirement Q(x) ≤ 1 in (3.2) which restricts the CFL condition (3.3) to μ = √3/2'). Hypotheses are in the sentence: TRUE both ways.

sentence: Suppose Q(x) is Lipschitz continuous and g_j satisfies (3.9a) (3.9b) then the numerical flux (3.8) satisfies (3.6)

scheme.definition: Modified 5-point flux (3.8): f̃_{j+1/2} = ½[f(v_j) + f(v_{j+1}) + (1/λ)(g_j + g_{j+1} - Q(ν_{j+1/2} + γ_{j+1/2}) Δ_{j+1/2}v)] (3.8d), γ_{j+1/2} = (g_{j+1} - g_j)/Δ_{j+1/2}v (3.8c). Second-order condition (3.6): f̃_{j+1/2} - f^{LW}_{j+1/2} = O(Δ^2) for all smooth solutions, f^{LW} the Lax-Wendroff flux (3.6a) with Q(x) = x^2.

justification: Proof pp. 15-16: (3.10a)-(3.10b) express f̃ - f^{LW}; by Lipschitz continuity (3.10c) the term [Q(ν) - Q(ν + γ)]Δv is O(Δ^2) by (3.9b), and (3.9a) gives the rest. The hypotheses are stated in the sentence, so TRUE both ways. Remark (2), p. 20 notes (3.6) is only necessary for second order accuracy; the sentence claims only (3.6).

sentence: Suppose Q(x) satisfies (3.2) and g_j is defined by (3.11), then the finite-difference scheme (1.4) with the numerical flux (3.8) is TVNI under the CFL restriction (3.3).

scheme.definition: 5-point scheme (1.4) with modified numerical flux (3.8d) and g_j from (3.11) (see Lemmas 3.2-3.3).

justification: The proof (pp. 18-19) applies Lemma 3.1 to the modified flux, which needs the modified CFL condition (3.14) |ν̃_{j+1/2}| = |ν + γ| ≤ μ, but it only shows |ν + γ| ≤ |ν| + ½[1 - ν^2] = 1 - ½(|ν| - 1)^2 ≤ 1. That closes the argument when (3.2) holds up to μ = 1 (e.g. Q(x) = |x|), but not when μ < 1: for Q(x) = x^2 + 1/4, μ = √3/2 (p. 32), (3.12) only gives |γ| ≤ 1/8, so the proof's bound allows |ν̃| above √3/2, where Q(ν̃) > 1 and Lemma 2.2's condition is not guaranteed. We found no counterexample either, and Osher-Tadmor (ot85, p. 3) report a CFL limitation 2/3 for their extension of this recipe 'in agreement with that found by Sweby'. The sentence contains its hypotheses, so the same verdict applies alone. UNSURE.

sentence: Suppose Q^k(x) satisfies (3.2) for all k, and that A(u) = A = constant, then the scheme (4.8) is TVNI under the CFL restriction λ max_k |a^k| ≤ μ = min_k μ_k (4.13) where μ_k are the restrictions in (3.2).

scheme.definition: System scheme (4.8) (see Lemma 4.1) in the constant coefficient case; TV of a vector mesh function defined by (4.12), TV(v) = Σ_j Σ_k |α^k_{j+1/2}|.

justification: Proof p. 26: with constant A the characteristic variables decouple and each satisfies the scalar scheme (3.8d)-(3.11), so the claim reduces to Lemma 3.4 per field. It therefore inherits the gap in Lemma 3.4's proof when some μ_k < 1 (the proof only bounds |ν + γ| by 1, not by μ_k; see harten_1982_highres:08). For fields with μ_k = 1 the argument closes. Hypotheses are in the sentence, so UNSURE both ways.

sentence: The scheme (4.8) in the constant coefficient case is convergent under the restriction (4.13) for all initial data of bounded total variation, and is second order accurate.

scheme.definition: System scheme (4.8) with A(u) = A constant (see Lemmas 4.1-4.2).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Q^k satisfy (3.2) (and are Lipschitz, Lemma 4.1).
Convergence argument: TVNI gives convergent subsequences, and in the constant coefficient case the solution is unique.
Second order in the sense of (3.6), possibly degenerating locally where u_x = 0.

justification: With hypotheses: convergence rests on the TV bound of Lemma 4.2 plus uniqueness for the linear problem (Remark (1), p. 19), so it inherits Lemma 4.2's gap when some μ_k < 1 (TRUE when all μ_k = 1); second order holds only in the formal sense of (3.6) away from points where u_x = 0 (Lemma 4.1; Remark (2), p. 20). UNSURE. Alone: 'second order accurate' without qualification is FALSE: the source says the scheme may degenerate to O(Δ^2) local truncation error at extrema (p. 20), and Osher-Tadmor 1985 (ot85, p. 15) show TVD schemes must give up second-order accuracy at nonsonic critical values (in the constant coefficient case every extremum is nonsonic).

sentence: Solutions of the upstream differencing scheme (5.1), under the CFL restriction λ max_{u∈Ω} |a(u)| ≤ 1, Ω = range of initial data, (5.2) have the monotonicity property stated at the beginning of Section 2.

scheme.definition: Scheme (3.5) with Q(x) = |x|: v_j^{n+1} = v_j - (ν_{j+1/2})^- Δ_{j+1/2}v^n - (ν_{j-1/2})^+ Δ_{j-1/2}v^n (5.1a), ν^- = min(ν, 0), ν^+ = max(ν, 0) (5.1b), ν_{j+1/2} = λ ā_{j+1/2}; a generalization of the Courant-Isaacson-Rees upstream scheme.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Monotonicity property (Section 2): (i) no new local extrema in x; (ii) local minima nondecreasing, local maxima nonincreasing.

justification: Only a 'Sketch of Proof' is given (p. 31): with W the piecewise-linear interpolant of v^n, (5.1) under (5.2) is said to give a monotone nondecreasing sequence x̃_j with v_j^{n+1} = W(x̃_j), which would imply the property; the step is asserted, not shown, and the scheme is otherwise referred to the literature ([5], [10]), which we did not read. The CFL restriction is part of the sentence, so the same verdict applies alone. UNSURE.

sentence: Then the following estimate holds: (2.10) E^{n+1} = E^n + (∆x/2) Σ_j (U^{n+1}_j − U^n_j)^2.

scheme.definition: Central scheme (2.7): (U^{n+1}_j − U^n_j)/∆t + a(U^n_{j+1} − U^n_{j−1})/(2∆x) = 0 for the linear transport equation U_t + aU_x = 0 (2.2), constant a; discrete energy (2.9): E^n = (1/2)∆x Σ_j (U^n_j)^2.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Let U^n_j be the solutions computed with the central scheme (2.7).
zero or periodic boundary conditions (used in the proof; 'a variant of the lemma holds for more general boundary conditions')
hypotheses.location: p. 15, proof of Lemma 2.3 and following paragraph

justification: With hypotheses: proved on pp. 14-15: multiplying (2.7) by U^n_j and using the identity (2.12) gives (2.13); multiplying by ∆x and summing, the flux terms H_{j+1/2} telescope and (2.10) follows exactly. Alone: the only omitted hypothesis is the boundary condition; for square-summable data on the whole grid Z the flux sum also telescopes, so the identity holds; it is an exact algebraic consequence of the scheme with no CFL or smoothness requirement.

sentence: Consequently, the energy grows at every time step for any choice of ∆x, ∆t.

scheme.definition: Central scheme (2.7): (U^{n+1}_j − U^n_j)/∆t + a(U^n_{j+1} − U^n_{j−1})/(2∆x) = 0 for U_t + aU_x = 0 (2.2); discrete energy (2.9): E^n = (1/2)∆x Σ_j (U^n_j)^2.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Let U^n_j be the solutions computed with the central scheme (2.7).
zero or periodic boundary conditions (used in the proof)

justification: Identity (2.10) (p. 14, proved p. 15) gives only E^{n+1} ⩾ E^n, with equality exactly when U^{n+1} = U^n. By (2.7) this happens whenever U^n_{j+1} = U^n_{j−1} for all j, e.g. constant data or the grid oscillation U^n_j = (−1)^j on a periodic grid with an even number of cells: then the energy stays the same, it does not grow. So the literal claim that the energy grows at every step, for any data, fails even with the periodic boundary conditions. Read as 'never decreases', or as 'grows for generic data', it would be TRUE; the notes' point (instability for every ∆x, ∆t) is right, but the sentence as written overstates it.

sentence: Then solutions computed with the upwind scheme (2.17) satisfy the energy estimate (2.19) E^{n+1} ⩽ E^n, where the energy is defined as in (2.9).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Let the mesh parameters satisfy the condition (2.18) |a| ∆t/∆x ⩽ 1.
zero or periodic boundary conditions (used in the proof)

justification: With hypotheses: proved pp. 17-18; summing (2.23) and substituting the scheme gives (2.25), E^{n+1} = E^n + (a^2∆t^2/(2∆x) − a∆t/2) Σ_j (U^n_j − U^n_{j−1})^2 (written there as ⩽), and the coefficient is ⩽ 0 exactly under (2.18). Alone (no CFL): the same identity shows the energy strictly increases for any non-constant data when |a|∆t/∆x > 1, and the notes' experiment with ∆t = 1.3∆x (Fig. 2.6(a), p. 16) is unstable; the notes call the scheme only 'conditionally stable'.

sentence: The upwind scheme is thus conditionally stable.

scheme.definition: Upwind scheme (2.17)/(2.16) for U_t + aU_x = 0 (2.2), as above; stability measured by the energy (2.9) E^n = (1/2)∆x Σ_j (U^n_j)^2.

hypotheses.hypothesis: the condition is the CFL condition (2.18) |a| ∆t/∆x ⩽ 1
zero or periodic boundary conditions (used in the proof)

justification: Energy stability E^{n+1} ⩽ E^n under (2.18) is proved on pp. 17-18 (via identity (2.25)), and the same identity shows energy growth when |a|∆t/∆x > 1, so stability holds under a condition and not unconditionally. The sentence itself carries the qualifier 'conditionally', so nothing is dropped when it is read alone.

sentence: Then solutions computed with the upwind scheme (2.17) satisfy the stability estimates (2.26) ‖U^{n+1}‖_{L1} ⩽ ‖U^n‖_{L1}, ‖U^{n+1}‖_{L∞} ⩽ ‖U^n‖_{L∞} ∀ n = 0, 1, 2, ..., where ‖U‖_{L1} = ∆x Σ_{j∈Z} |U_j| and ‖U‖_{L∞} = sup_{j∈N} |U_j|.

scheme.definition: Upwind scheme (2.17)/(2.16) for U_t + aU_x = 0 (2.2): with ν = ∆t/∆x, U^{n+1}_j = U^n_{j+1}(−νa−) + U^n_j(1 − ν|a|) + U^n_{j−1}νa+.
scheme.location: eqs. (2.16)-(2.17), p. 15; rewritten form in the proof, p. 18

hypotheses.hypothesis: Assume that the CFL condition (2.18) |a|∆t/∆x ⩽ 1 is satisfied.

justification: With hypotheses: proved p. 18; under (2.18) the coefficients −νa−, 1 − ν|a|, νa+ are non-negative and sum to 1, so U^{n+1}_j is a convex combination of neighbours, giving both bounds. Alone: without the CFL condition the middle coefficient 1 − ν|a| is negative; e.g. a > 0, νa = 2 and a single nonzero value U^n_0 = 1 give U^{n+1}_0 = −1, U^{n+1}_1 = 2, so both the L1 norm (×3) and the L∞ norm (×2) grow.

sentence: Then (4.39) is conservative if and only if there exists a function F^n_{j+1/2} = F(U^n_{j−p+1}, ..., U^n_{j+p}) such that (4.39) can be written in the finite volume form (4.14).

scheme.definition: Generic (2p+1)-point scheme (4.39): U^{n+1}_j = H(U^n_{j−p}, ..., U^n_{j+p}); conservative (Definition 4.4): ignoring boundary conditions, Σ_j U^{n+1}_j = Σ_j U^n_j for all n (4.40); finite volume form (4.14): U^{n+1}_j = U^n_j − (∆t/∆x)(F^n_{j+1/2} − F^n_{j−1/2}).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Assume that H(0, ..., 0) = 0.
boundary conditions ignored (whole-line grid)

justification: With hypotheses: proved p. 49: the flux form telescopes to give (4.40); conversely F_{1/2} is constructed explicitly from G = (∆x/∆t)(U_0 − H) using compactly supported data, which is where H(0,...,0) = 0 makes the sums finite. Alone: the assumption is harmless, since any scheme in flux form has H(0,...,0) = 0 automatically, and a scheme with H(0,...,0) ≠ 0 cannot satisfy (4.40) on compactly supported data (the sum Σ_j U^{n+1}_j would diverge), so the equivalence holds without stating it.

sentence: Then the method (4.14) is monotone if and only if (4.44) a ↦ F(a,b) is non-decreasing for fixed b, b ↦ F(a,b) is non-increasing for fixed a, and the following CFL-type condition holds: (4.45) |∂F/∂a (v,w)| + |∂F/∂b (u,v)| ⩽ ∆x/∆t ∀ u,v,w.

scheme.definition: Finite volume scheme (4.14): U^{n+1}_j = U^n_j − (∆t/∆x)(F(U^n_j,U^n_{j+1}) − F(U^n_{j−1},U^n_j)) with a two-point flux F = F(a,b); monotone (Definition 4.7): the update function H of (4.39) is non-decreasing in each of its arguments.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Consider the finite volume scheme (4.14) with a locally Lipschitz continuous two-point flux F = F(a,b).

justification: The notes leave the proof as an exercise (p. 50), so this rests on a direct check: H(a,b,c) = b − (∆t/∆x)(F(b,c) − F(a,b)) has ∂H/∂a = (∆t/∆x)∂F/∂a(a,b), ∂H/∂c = −(∆t/∆x)∂F/∂b(b,c), ∂H/∂b = 1 − (∆t/∆x)(∂F/∂a(b,c) − ∂F/∂b(a,b)); non-negativity of these for all a,b,c is exactly (4.44) plus (4.45) once the signs from (4.44) turn the bracket into |∂F/∂a(v,w)| + |∂F/∂b(u,v)|. For a locally Lipschitz F the derivatives exist almost everywhere and the conditions are read a.e.; that does not change the equivalence. The hypothesis is inside the sentence's setting (the scheme field), so alone is the same.

sentence: Then the solutions satisfy (4.47) min(U^n_{j−1}, U^n_j, U^n_{j+1}) ⩽ U^{n+1}_j ⩽ max(U^n_{j−1}, U^n_j, U^n_{j+1}) for all n,j.

scheme.definition: Three-point scheme (4.46): U^{n+1}_j = H(U^n_{j−1}, U^n_j, U^n_{j+1}), the finite volume scheme (4.14) written in update form; consistency gives H(U,U,U) = U; monotone: H non-decreasing in each of its three arguments.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Let U^n_j be the approximate solutions generated by a three-point consistent monotone scheme of the form (4.46).

justification: Proved p. 51: replacing each argument of H by the local maximum one at a time uses monotonicity, and H(Ū,Ū,Ū) = Ū uses consistency; the minimum is analogous. The scheme class in the sentence's setting already contains every hypothesis (monotonicity implicitly includes the CFL-type condition, cf. Lemma 4.8), so nothing is dropped.

sentence: In particular, we have (4.48) min_i U^0_i ⩽ U^n_j ⩽ max_i U^0_i for all n,j.

scheme.definition: Three-point consistent monotone scheme (4.46): U^{n+1}_j = H(U^n_{j−1}, U^n_j, U^n_{j+1}), H(U,U,U) = U, H non-decreasing in each argument.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Let U^n_j be the approximate solutions generated by a three-point consistent monotone scheme of the form (4.46).

justification: Proved p. 51 by iterating (4.47) over the time levels. (For infinitely many cells read min/max as inf/sup.) No hypothesis beyond the scheme class is used.

sentence: Then U satisfies the discrete entropy inequality (4.50) |U^{n+1}_j − k| − |U^n_j − k| + (∆t/∆x)(Q^n_{j+1/2} − Q^n_{j−1/2}) ⩽ 0 for all n,j.

scheme.definition: Consistent, conservative, monotone three-point scheme (4.46)/(4.14): U^{n+1}_j = H(U^n_{j−1},U^n_j,U^n_{j+1}) = U^n_j − (∆t/∆x)(F(U^n_j,U^n_{j+1}) − F(U^n_{j−1},U^n_j)); Crandall–Majda numerical entropy flux (4.49): Q^n_{j+1/2} = F(U^n_j ∨ k, U^n_{j+1} ∨ k) − F(U^n_j ∧ k, U^n_{j+1} ∧ k), for a constant k ∈ R, a∨b = max(a,b), a∧b = min(a,b).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Let U^n_j be an approximate solution computed by a consistent, conservative and monotone three-point scheme (4.46).
k ∈ R an arbitrary constant

justification: Proved p. 52: H(U∨k) − H(U∧k) equals |U^n_j − k| − (∆t/∆x)(Q_{j+1/2} − Q_{j−1/2}) by the flux form, and monotonicity plus consistency give H(U∨k) ⩾ max(U^{n+1}_j, k) and H(U∧k) ⩽ min(U^{n+1}_j, k) (the text layer prints '>' for '⩾' in (4.53)-(4.54)). This is the Crandall–Majda (1980) result the notes cite. All hypotheses are in the sentence's scheme class.

sentence: In particular, if U0 ∈ L1(R) then (4.51) Σ_j |U^n_j| ∆x ⩽ ‖U0‖_{L1(R)} ∀ n ∈ N.

scheme.definition: Consistent, conservative, monotone three-point scheme (4.46)/(4.14) with initial cell averages (4.4): U^0_j = (1/∆x) ∫_{C_j} U0(x) dx.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Let U^n_j be an approximate solution computed by a consistent, conservative and monotone three-point scheme (4.46).

justification: Proof p. 52: set k = 0 in (4.50) and sum over j; Q(0,0) = 0 so the entropy flux differences telescope for l1 data, giving Σ_j |U^{n+1}_j| ⩽ Σ_j |U^n_j|; and Σ_j |U^0_j| ∆x ⩽ ‖U0‖_{L1} because the U^0_j are cell averages (4.4). The L1 assumption is in the sentence.

sentence: (i) If the coefficients satisfy (4.57) C^n_{j+1/2}, D^n_{j+1/2} ⩾ 0 and C^n_{j+1/2} + D^n_{j+1/2} ⩽ 1 for all n,j then solutions computed with (4.55) are TVD, i.e. they satisfy (4.58) Σ_j |U^{n+1}_{j+1} − U^{n+1}_j| ⩽ Σ_j |U^n_{j+1} − U^n_j| for all n.

scheme.definition: Incremental form (4.55): U^{n+1}_j = U^n_j + C^n_{j+1/2}(U^n_{j+1} − U^n_j) − D^n_{j−1/2}(U^n_j − U^n_{j−1}); for the finite volume scheme (4.14) the coefficients are (4.56): C^n_{j+1/2} = (∆t/∆x)(f(U^n_j) − F^n_{j+1/2})/(U^n_{j+1} − U^n_j), D^n_{j+1/2} = (∆t/∆x)(f(U^n_{j+1}) − F^n_{j+1/2})/(U^n_{j+1} − U^n_j).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Consider the scheme (4.55).

justification: Proved p. 53: U^{n+1}_{j+1} − U^{n+1}_j = (1 − C_{j+1/2} − D_{j+1/2})∆_{j+1/2} + C_{j+3/2}∆_{j+3/2} + D_{j−1/2}∆_{j−1/2} with non-negative coefficients under (4.57); summing absolute values, each |∆_{j+1/2}| gets total weight 1. This is Harten's lemma (Harten 1983, cited as [Har83]); Gottlieb and Shu 1998 (gs98, p. 74) also cite it. The coefficient condition is in the sentence. The inequality sign is '⩾ 0' in the second text extraction (source mfa_oslo_notes); the page-marked file prints '> 0'.

sentence: (ii) If the coefficients satisfy (4.59) C^n_{j+1/2}, D^n_{j+1/2} ⩾ 0 and C^n_{j+1/2} + D^n_{j−1/2} ⩽ 1 for all n,j then ‖U^{n+1}‖_{L∞} ⩽ ‖U^n‖_{L∞} for all n.

scheme.definition: Incremental form (4.55): U^{n+1}_j = U^n_j + C^n_{j+1/2}(U^n_{j+1} − U^n_j) − D^n_{j−1/2}(U^n_j − U^n_{j−1}).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Consider the scheme (4.55).

justification: Proved p. 53: U^{n+1}_j = C_{j+1/2}U^n_{j+1} + (1 − C_{j+1/2} − D_{j−1/2})U^n_j + D_{j−1/2}U^n_{j−1}, a convex combination under (4.59), so |U^{n+1}_j| ⩽ max of neighbours. The condition is in the sentence.

sentence: Any consistent and conservative monotone three-point finite volume scheme (4.14) is TVD under the CFL condition (4.45), i.e., it satisfies (4.58).

scheme.definition: Finite volume scheme (4.14): U^{n+1}_j = U^n_j − (∆t/∆x)(F(U^n_j,U^n_{j+1}) − F(U^n_{j−1},U^n_j)), consistent F(U,U) = f(U) (4.43), monotone (Definition 4.7: update H non-decreasing in each argument); TVD means (4.58) Σ_j |U^{n+1}_{j+1} − U^{n+1}_j| ⩽ Σ_j |U^n_{j+1} − U^n_j|.

hypotheses.hypothesis: CFL condition (4.45): |∂F/∂a(v,w)| + |∂F/∂b(u,v)| ⩽ ∆x/∆t for all u,v,w
Lipschitz numerical flux (used in the proof)

justification: Proof pp. 53-54 checks Harten's conditions (4.57): C, D ⩾ 0 from consistency and the monotonicity signs of F. Its bound C + D ⩽ 1 via (4.45) is loose (the derivatives are evaluated at points that do not share an argument as (4.45) requires), but the bound follows directly from monotonicity: H(U_j,·,U_{j+1}) non-decreasing in the middle argument, compared at U_j and U_{j+1}, gives exactly (C_{j+1/2} + D_{j+1/2})(U_{j+1} − U_j) ⩽ U_{j+1} − U_j. So the claim holds; the CFL condition is part of monotonicity (Lemma 4.8) and is in the sentence anyway.

sentence: Then {U^n_j} satisfies the time continuity property (4.60) Σ_{j∈Z} |U^n_j − U^m_j| ∆x ⩽ |t_n − t_m| C_F ‖U0‖_{TV(R)} where C_F is the Lipschitz constant of F.

scheme.definition: Consistent, conservative, monotone finite volume scheme (4.14) (the statement says '(4.1)', evidently meaning (4.14)): U^{n+1}_j = U^n_j − (∆t/∆x)(F(U^n_j,U^n_{j+1}) − F(U^n_{j−1},U^n_j)), with U^0_j the cell averages (4.4).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Let {U^n_j} be computed with a consistent and conservative monotone scheme (4.1) with a Lipschitz continuous numerical flux function F = F(a,b).

justification: The proof (pp. 54-55) bounds one step by ∆t(‖∂F/∂a‖_∞ + ‖∂F/∂b‖_∞)‖U^n‖_TV and then writes this as ∆t C_F ‖U^n‖_TV, which needs C_F ⩾ ‖∂F/∂a‖ + ‖∂F/∂b‖; for the usual Lipschitz constant (Euclidean, or the convention |F(a,b) − F(c,d)| ⩽ C_F(|a−c| + |b−d|) the notes use for Q on p. 57) this fails. Counterexample: f ≡ 0, Lax–Friedrichs flux (4.30) F(a,b) = −(∆x/(2∆t))(b − a), monotone and consistent, so U^{n+1}_j = (U^n_{j+1} + U^n_{j−1})/2; with U^0_j = 1 for j ⩽ 0 and 0 for j ⩾ 1 (TV = 1), one step gives Σ_j |U^1_j − U^0_j| ∆x = ∆x, while ∆t C_F ‖U0‖_TV = ∆x/2 (l1 convention, C_F = ∆x/(2∆t)) or ∆x/√2 (Euclidean). The estimate does hold with 2C_F, or with C_F read as the Lipschitz constant for the max norm on (a,b).

sentence: Then U is a weak solution of (4.1), with initial data U0.

scheme.definition: Conservative and consistent finite volume scheme (4.14): U^{n+1}_j = U^n_j − (∆t/∆x)(F^n_{j+1/2} − F^n_{j−1/2}) with a differentiable (or Lipschitz) numerical flux F, F(U,...,U) = f(U), initial cell averages (4.4); U^{∆x}(x,t) = U^n_j on [x_{j−1/2}, x_{j+1/2}) × [t^n, t^{n+1}) (4.61).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Let U^n_j be approximate solutions of (4.1), computed by a conservative and consistent finite volume scheme (4.14) with a differentiable (or Lipschitz) numerical flux function F, where U^0_j is given by (4.4).

Assume that U0 ∈ L∞(R) and that the approximating functions U^{∆x} are uniformly bounded, ‖U^{∆x}‖_{L∞(R×R+)} ⩽ C for all ∆x > 0 (4.62), and converge in L1_loc(R × R+) as ∆x, ∆t → 0 to some function U.

justification: With hypotheses: the Lax–Wendroff theorem, proved pp. 55-56 by summation by parts against a test function; Shu's ICASE notes (C.-W. Shu, 'Essentially non-oscillatory and weighted essentially non-oscillatory schemes for hyperbolic conservation laws', 1997; shu97nd, pdf p. 22) state the same: 'by the classic Lax-Wendroff theorem [51], the solution to the conservative scheme (2.68), if converges, will converge to a weak solution of (2.65)'. Alone: the sentence's 'U' is the limit whose existence is a dropped hypothesis; without assuming convergence the sentence has no definite content (and unstable conservative consistent schemes such as the central flux (4.37), p. 48, do not converge at all), so I cannot assign it a truth value by itself.

sentence: Then U = lim_{∆x→0} U^{∆x} is the entropy solution of (3.4).

scheme.definition: Conservative and consistent finite volume scheme (4.14) with Lipschitz numerical flux F, satisfying the discrete entropy inequality (4.50) with the Crandall–Majda entropy flux (4.49): Q^n_{j+1/2} = F(U^n_j ∨ k, U^n_{j+1} ∨ k) − F(U^n_j ∧ k, U^n_{j+1} ∧ k).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Assume that the conditions of the Lax–Wendroff theorem hold (conservative consistent scheme with Lipschitz flux, U0 ∈ L∞, U^{∆x} uniformly bounded and convergent in L1_loc)
and in addition that the discrete entropy inequality (4.50) holds (for all k ∈ R)

justification: The notes do not write the proof ('By applying the same technique as for the Lax–Wendroff theorem, we can easily prove', p. 56), but the argument is the Lax–Wendroff summation by parts (pp. 55-56) applied to (4.50) with a non-negative test function, using that Q is Lipschitz and consistent with the Kruzkov entropy flux, Q(U,U) = q(U,k) (shown p. 52); this gives the Kruzkov entropy condition, which characterises entropy solutions (Lemma 3.7, p. 30). I mark it TRUE on that basis, not on a written proof in the source. Alone: as with item 16 the limit U is defined only through the dropped convergence hypothesis, so the sentence by itself is not settled.

sentence: Then U^{∆x} → U in L1(R × [0,T]) as ∆x, ∆t → 0 for any T > 0, where U is the entropy solution of (3.4)

scheme.definition: Consistent, conservative and monotone finite volume method (4.14) with a locally Lipschitz flux F for U_t + f(U)_x = 0 (4.1); U^{∆x}(x,t) = ((t^{n+1} − t)/∆t)U^n_j + ((t − t^n)/∆t)U^{n+1}_j for x ∈ C_j, t ∈ [t^n, t^{n+1}).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Consider the scalar conservation law (4.1) with f ∈ C1(R) and U0 ∈ BV(R) (with ‖U‖_BV = ‖U‖_L1 + ‖U‖_TV, p. 57).
Consider a consistent, conservative and monotone finite volume method (4.14) with a locally Lipschitz continuous flux F.
Assume, in addition to the CFL condition (4.45), that there is some c > 0 such that (4.67) ∆t/∆x ⩾ c.
hypotheses.location: p. 57, Theorem 4.19 (the page-marked file prints '>' , source mfa_oslo_notes prints '⩾')

justification: With hypotheses: proved p. 57 by Helly's theorem (BV and L1 bounds from Lemmas 4.10, 4.13, tail control from the maximum principle and (4.67)), Ascoli's theorem with the time continuity (4.60), Lemma 4.16 and uniqueness of the entropy solution; this is the Crandall–Majda (1980) convergence theorem the notes cite. The constant error in Lemma 4.14 (item 15) only changes C_F to 2C_F and does not affect the argument. Alone: the sentence drops f ∈ C1, U0 ∈ BV and the lower bound (4.67) on ∆t/∆x (monotonicity, and with it the CFL condition, is part of the scheme). Whether the L1(R × [0,T]) convergence holds for general data or without (4.67) is not settled by what I read.

sentence: Then the scheme is at least first-order accurate.

scheme.definition: Consistent and conservative three-point finite volume method (4.14)/(4.46): U^{n+1}_j = H(U^n_{j−1},U^n_j,U^n_{j+1}) = U^n_j − (∆t/∆x)(F(U^n_j,U^n_{j+1}) − F(U^n_{j−1},U^n_j)); order of accuracy (Definition 5.1): with ∆t/∆x ≡ λ fixed, truncation error T^n_j = U(x_j,t^{n+1}) − H(U(x_{j−1},t^n), U(x_j,t^n), U(x_{j+1},t^n)) (5.5), q-th order if q is the largest integer with T^n_j = O(∆t^{q+1}) for all j,n as ∆t → 0 (5.6).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Assume that the exact solution U(x,t) of the scalar conservation law is C2, and that a consistent and conservative three-point finite volume method has a C2 update function H.
∆t/∆x ≡ λ for some constant λ > 0

justification: With hypotheses: proved p. 61 by Taylor expansion, consistency and the PDE U_t + f'(U)U_x = 0, giving T^n_j = O(∆t^2) (uniformity in j,n implicitly needs bounded second derivatives). Alone: without a C2 exact solution the truncation error need not be O(∆t^2). Example: the upwind scheme (2.16), i.e. Godunov for a linear flux, which has a linear (C2) H, for U_t + U_x = 0 with λ = 1/2 and a step that at t^n sits at x_j − ∆x/4 (left value 1, right 0) gives U(x_j,t^{n+1}) = 1 but H = (1/2)·0 + (1/2)·1 = 1/2, so T^n_j = 1/2 = O(1). The notes themselves (p. 62) say the lemma does not directly apply to the non-C2 Godunov flux.

sentence: If the discrete differential operator L is such that the forward Euler method (5.44) is TVD, then the Runge–Kutta method (5.47) is TVD.

scheme.definition: Semi-discrete scheme (5.43) dU/dt = L(U), L(U)_j = −(1/∆x)(F_{j+1/2} − F_{j−1/2}); forward Euler (5.44): U^{n+1} = U^n + ∆t L(U^n); TVD (5.45): TV(U^{n+1}) ⩽ TV(U^n) for all n; second-order SSP Runge–Kutta (5.47): U* = U^n + ∆t L(U^n), U** = U* + ∆t L(U*), U^{n+1} = (1/2)(U^n + U**).

hypotheses.hypothesis: forward Euler (5.44) is TVD (with the same time step ∆t, for any input vector)

justification: Proved p. 76: both stages are forward Euler steps, so TV(U**) ⩽ TV(U*) ⩽ TV(U^n), and TV is a seminorm, so TV((U^n + U**)/2) ⩽ TV(U^n). This agrees with S. Gottlieb and C.-W. Shu, 'Total variation diminishing Runge-Kutta schemes', Math. Comp. 67 (1998) 73-85 (gs98, Lemma 1.1, p. 74, and Proposition 3.1, p. 78), where this method is the optimal second-order TVD Runge–Kutta method with CFL coefficient 1. The hypothesis is in the sentence.

sentence: We design arbitrarily high-order accurate entropy stable schemes for systems of conservation laws.

scheme.definition: TeCNO schemes: semidiscrete conservative scheme d/dt u_i = -(1/Δx)(F_{i+1/2} - F_{i-1/2}) (1.6) with flux F^k_{i+1/2} = ~F^{2p}_{i+1/2} - (1/2) D_{i+1/2} ⟨⟨v⟩⟩_{i+1/2} (3.8), p = k/2 (k even) or (k+1)/2 (k odd); ~F^{2p}_{i+1/2} = sum_{r=1}^{p} α^p_r sum_{s=0}^{r-1} ~F(u_{i-s}, u_{i-s+r}) (2.20) (e.g. ~F^4 = (4/3)~F(u_i,u_{i+1}) - (1/6)(~F(u_{i-1},u_{i+1}) + ~F(u_i,u_{i+2})) (2.22)), built from a consistent two-point entropy conservative flux satisfying [[v]]^T ~F = [[ψ]] (2.2); D_{i+1/2} = R Λ R^T (3.4)/(3.9) with R eigenvectors of ∂_u f and Λ Roe-type diag(|λ_1|,...,|λ_m|) (3.5) or Rusanov-type max|λ| I (3.6); ⟨⟨v⟩⟩_{i+1/2} = v^-_{i+1} - v^+_i from a k-th order ENO reconstruction of the scaled entropy variables w^±_i = R^T_{i±1/2} v_i (Sec. 3.5). v = ∂_u E for a convex entropy E with entropy flux Q, ψ = v^T f - Q.

hypotheses.hypothesis: The system has a convex entropy E with entropy flux Q
Accuracy for smooth solutions, proven order (k-1) for k-th order ENO reconstruction
Entropy stability is for the semidiscrete scheme (1.6): discrete entropy inequality (3.11)

justification: Theorem 4.1 (p. 556, with proof) gives, for every k ≥ 1, (k-1)th order accuracy for smooth solutions and entropy stability of the semidiscrete scheme; since k is arbitrary, the schemes are arbitrarily high-order accurate. Entropy stability rests on Lemma 3.2 (proof p. 553) and Corollary 3.5, i.e. on the ENO sign property (Theorem 3.4, proved in the cited [10]); accuracy rests on the cited Theorem 2.2(i) with the coefficient normalization of (2.22)-(2.23) (see item :03). The omitted hypotheses are harmless for the default reading: order of accuracy refers to smooth solutions, and 'entropy stable' presupposes an entropy pair; the scheme as defined is semidiscrete.

sentence: Then the scheme with numerical flux ~F_{i+1/2} is second-order accurate and entropy conservative—solutions computed by the scheme satisfy the discrete entropy equality (2.1) with numerical entropy flux (2.3) ~Q_{i+1/2} = v_{i+1/2}^T ~F_{i+1/2} − ψ_{i+1/2}.

scheme.definition: Semidiscrete conservative scheme d/dt u_i = -(1/Δx)(~F_{i+1/2} - ~F_{i-1/2}) (1.6) with a consistent two-point flux ~F_{i+1/2} satisfying [[v]]^T_{i+1/2} ~F_{i+1/2} = [[ψ]]_{i+1/2} (2.2), where [[a]]_{i+1/2} = a_{i+1} - a_i and the bar (average) a_{i+1/2} = (a_i + a_{i+1})/2 (the overbar on v and ψ in (2.3) is lost in the text layer).

hypotheses.hypothesis: ~F_{i+1/2} is a consistent numerical flux satisfying (2.2)
Existence of a convex entropy pair (E, Q), entropy variables v, potential ψ = v^T f - Q

justification: Entropy conservation follows directly from (2.2) (multiply (1.6) by v_i^T; standard and consistent with Tadmor 1987). Second-order accuracy is proved by Tadmor (E. Tadmor, 'The numerical viscosity of entropy stable schemes for systems of conservation laws. I', Math. Comp. 49 (1987) 91-103, Sec. 4, scheme (4.9), via the trapezoidal rule; source tadmor_1987_viscosity) for his path-integral flux (2.5), and for scalar laws the flux (2.7) is unique; it is not proved here for every consistent solution of (2.2). For m ≥ 2, solutions of (2.2) are not unique (p. 547), and our own check suggests a counterexample: for f(u) = Au with A symmetric, ~F = (1/2)A(u_i + u_{i+1}) + K(u_{i+1} - u_i) with K constant antisymmetric is consistent and satisfies (2.2), but adds K u_xx Δx to the truncation error (first order). This is not a published counterexample, so we leave both readings UNSURE.

sentence: Then the finite difference scheme with flux ~F^{2p} is (i) 2pth-order accurate, in the sense that for sufficiently smooth solutions u we have (1/Δx)(~F^{2p}(u_{i−p+1},...,u_{i+p}) − ~F^{2p}(u_{i−p},...,u_{i+p−1})) = ∂_x f(u_i) + O(Δx^{2p}); (ii) entropy conservative—it satisfies the discrete entropy identity d/dt E(u_i(t)) + (1/Δx)(~Q^{2p}_{i+1/2} − ~Q^{2p}_{i−1/2}) = 0, where (2.21) ~Q^{2p}_{i+1/2} = sum_{r=1}^{p} α^p_r sum_{s=0}^{r−1} ~Q(u_{i−s}, u_{i−s+r}).

scheme.definition: Semidiscrete scheme (1.6) with flux ~F^{2p}_{i+1/2} = sum_{r=1}^{p} α^p_r sum_{s=0}^{r-1} ~F(u_{i-s}, u_{i-s+r}) (2.20), ~F a two-point entropy conservative flux satisfying (2.2); examples p = 2: α = (4/3, -1/6) (2.22); p = 3: α = (3/2, -3/10, 1/30) (2.23).

hypotheses.hypothesis: α^p_1, ..., α^p_p solve the p linear equations 2 sum_{r=1}^{p} r α^p_r = 1, sum_{i=1}^{p} i^{2s-1} α^p_r = 0 (s = 2, ..., p) (as printed)
~F is a consistent two-point flux satisfying (2.2)
Sufficiently smooth solutions u (for (i))

justification: With the hypotheses as printed: for p = 1 the condition 2 sum r α_r = 1 forces α^1_1 = 1/2, so ~F^2 = (1/2)~F(u_i, u_{i+1}) and the flux difference approximates (1/2)∂_x f, contradicting (i); the paper's own examples (2.22) (sum r α_r = 4/3 - 2/6 = 1) and (2.23) (3/2 - 6/10 + 3/30 = 1) satisfy sum r α_r = 1, not 2 sum r α_r = 1, so the printed normalization makes (i) false (part (ii) holds for any α by telescoping). Alone (with α as in (2.22)-(2.23)): the proof is in LeFloch, Mercier and Rohde [19, Thm 4.4], which we did not read, and part (i) seems to need a symmetric two-point flux (same construction as in item :02), so UNSURE.

sentence: The scheme with flux (3.2) is entropy stable—its solutions satisfy (3.3) d/dt E(u_i) + (1/Δx)(^Q_{i+1/2} − ^Q_{i−1/2}) = −(1/(4Δx))([[v]]^T_{i+1/2} D_{i+1/2} [[v]]_{i+1/2} + [[v]]^T_{i−1/2} D_{i−1/2} [[v]]_{i−1/2}) ≤ 0, where ^Q_{i+1/2} = ~Q_{i+1/2} + (1/2) v^T_{i+1/2} D_{i+1/2} [[v]]_{i+1/2} and ~Q_{i+1/2} is the numerical entropy flux function of the flux ~F_{i+1/2}.

scheme.definition: Semidiscrete scheme (1.6) with first-order entropy stable flux F_{i+1/2} = ~F_{i+1/2} - (1/2) D_{i+1/2} [[v]]_{i+1/2} (3.2), ~F the second-order entropy conservative flux satisfying (2.2), D any symmetric positive definite matrix; v_{i+1/2} in ^Q denotes the interface average (overbar lost in the text layer).

hypotheses.hypothesis: D_{i+1/2} symmetric positive definite
~F consistent and satisfies (2.2)

justification: Entropy stability itself is true: the proof of Lemma 3.2 (p. 553) with ⟨⟨v⟩⟩ = [[v]] gives (3.3) with ^Q_{i+1/2} = ~Q_{i+1/2} − (1/2) v^T_{i+1/2} D [[v]]_{i+1/2}, the sign printed in Lemma 3.2 (p. 552). The sentence, however, defines ^Q with a plus sign, and with that sign the identity (3.3) is false: e.g. scalar f ≡ 0 (so ~F = ~Q = 0), E = u^2/2, D = 1, data u_{i-1} = u_i = 0, u_{i+1} = 1: the scheme gives d/dt E(u_i) = 0, while (3.3) with the printed ^Q would require d/dt E(u_i) = -1/(2Δx) (with the minus sign it requires 0, as it should). As stated, the sentence is false both alone and with its hypotheses; the error is only the sign in the printed entropy flux.

sentence: Then the scheme with numerical flux (3.8) is entropy stable—its computed solutions satisfy the entropy dissipation estimate (3.11) d/dt E(u_i) + (1/Δx)(^Q^k_{i+1/2} − ^Q^k_{i−1/2}) ≤ 0, where the numerical entropy flux function ^Q^k is defined as ^Q^k_{i+1/2} = ~Q^{2p}_{i+1/2} − (1/2) v^T_{i+1/2} D_{i+1/2} ⟨⟨v⟩⟩_{i+1/2} and ~Q^{2p} is defined in (2.21).

scheme.definition: Semidiscrete scheme (1.6) with flux F^k_{i+1/2} = ~F^{2p}_{i+1/2} - (1/2) D_{i+1/2} ⟨⟨v⟩⟩_{i+1/2} (3.8), ⟨⟨v⟩⟩_{i+1/2} = v^-_{i+1} - v^+_i (3.7) from a piecewise polynomial reconstruction v_i(x) of the entropy variables, ~F^{2p} from (2.20).

hypotheses.hypothesis: R_{i+1/2} nonsingular, Λ_{i+1/2} nonnegative diagonal, D_{i+1/2} = R Λ R^T (3.9)
The reconstruction satisfies ⟨⟨v⟩⟩_{i+1/2} = (R^T_{i+1/2})^{-1} B_{i+1/2} R^T_{i+1/2} [[v]]_{i+1/2} with a diagonal B_{i+1/2} ≥ 0 (3.10)
~F^{2p} entropy conservative (Theorem 2.2(ii))

justification: Alone (flux (3.8) with an arbitrary reconstruction): the paper states on p. 552 that 'the scheme with numerical flux (3.8) might not be entropy stable. We need to modify the reconstruction procedure', i.e. the sign condition (3.10) is needed. With hypotheses: the proof on p. 553 multiplies (1.6) by v_i^T, uses entropy conservation of ~F^{2p}, and shows [[v]]^T D ⟨⟨v⟩⟩ = (R^T[[v]])^T Λ B (R^T[[v]]) ≥ 0 (the printed intermediate 'RΛR^{-1}RBR^T' should read RΛR^T(R^T)^{-1}BR^T; the result is unchanged). Entropy conservation of ~F^{2p} holds for any coefficients α by telescoping. The claim is for the semidiscrete scheme.

sentence: Then the reconstruction satisfies the sign property: (3.17) sign(ω^−_{i+1} − ω^+_i) = sign(ω_{i+1} − ω_i).

scheme.definition: k-th order ENO reconstruction of point values ω_i: select a stencil {x_{i-r_i}, ..., x_{i-1-r_i+k}} with left shift r_i ∈ {0, ..., k-1} determined from the undivided differences, interpolate, and evaluate at the cell interfaces to get ω^+_i, ω^-_{i+1} (Harten et al. [13]).
scheme.location: Sec. 3.5, p. 555; defined in Harten, Engquist, Osher, Chakravarthy [13] as cited on p. 555

justification: The theorem is quoted from [10] (Fjordholm, Mishra, Tadmor, 'ENO reconstruction and ENO interpolation are stable', Found. Comput. Math., in press as cited) and is not proved in this paper. The paper only checks the case k = 2 (Sec. 3.4, p. 555: the second-order ENO limiter (3.16) is symmetric with φ ≤ 1, which gives the sign property). We did not read [10], so nothing we read settles the general-k claim.

sentence: Furthermore, we have (3.18) (ω^−_{i+1} − ω^+_i)/(ω_{i+1} − ω_i) ≤ C_k for a constant C_k that only depends on k.

scheme.definition: k-th order ENO reconstruction of point values ω_i as in Sec. 3.5 (Harten et al. [13]).
