justification: The upper jump bound is quoted from [10] without proof in this paper (it is used in the proof of Theorem 4.3, p. 557). We did not read [10]; for k = 2 the ENO limiter φ ≤ 1 with φ(θ) ≥ -1 gives ⟨⟨w⟩⟩ = (1 - (φ + φ)/2)δ with ratio at most 2 (Sec. 3.4, p. 554-555), consistent with the claim, but the general case is not settled by what we read.

sentence: The reconstructed values ~w^±_i satisfy the sign property (3.12).

scheme.definition: ENO reconstruction in scaled entropy variables: w^±_i = R^T_{i±1/2} v_i; for each cell define μ^i_i = w^-_i, ν^i_i = w^+_i and extend with the jumps δ_{j+1/2} = ⟨⟨w⟩⟩_{j+1/2}; choose the ENO stencil from these differences; p_i, q_i the interpolants of μ^i, ν^i; ~w^-_i = p_i(x_{i-1/2}), ~w^+_i = q_i(x_{i+1/2}); v^±_i = (R^T_{i±1/2})^{-1} ~w^±_i.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Theorem 3.4 (ENO sign property) holds

justification: The proof (p. 556) identifies q_i with the standard ENO polynomial h_i of the data μ^{i+1} (by (3.20)) and p_{i+1} = h_{i+1}, so ⟨⟨~w⟩⟩_{i+1/2} = h_{i+1}(x_{i+1/2}) - h_i(x_{i+1/2}), which by Theorem 3.4 has the sign of μ^{i+1}_{i+1} - μ^{i+1}_i = ⟨⟨w⟩⟩_{i+1/2}. The argument is complete given Theorem 3.4 (proved in the cited [10]). The sentence refers to the reconstruction just defined, so alone and with hypotheses agree.

sentence: Then the finite difference scheme with numerical flux (3.8) is (i) (k − 1)th-order accurate for smooth solutions, (ii) entropy stable—computed solutions satisfy the discrete entropy inequality (3.11).

scheme.definition: TeCNO scheme: (1.6) with flux (3.8) F^k_{i+1/2} = ~F^{2p}_{i+1/2} - (1/2) D_{i+1/2} ⟨⟨v⟩⟩_{i+1/2}, ~F^{2p} from (2.20), 2p = k (k even) or k+1 (k odd), D = RΛR^T (3.9), ⟨⟨v⟩⟩ from the k-th order ENO reconstruction of scaled entropy variables (Sec. 3.5).

hypotheses.hypothesis: k ≥ 1; 2p = k (k even) or 2p = k+1 (k odd); ~F^{2p} defined by (2.20)
⟨⟨v⟩⟩ from the k-th order ENO reconstruction procedure of Sec. 3.5
R_{i+1/2} nonsingular, Λ_{i+1/2} ≥ 0 diagonal (Lemma 3.2)
Smooth solutions for (i)

justification: Proof p. 556: (i) ⟨⟨~w⟩⟩_{i+1/2} = (h_{i+1} - h_i)(x_{i+1/2}) = O(Δx^k), so the diffusion term contributes O(Δx^{k-1}) to the truncation error, and ~F^{2p} with 2p ≥ k is of order ≥ k by Theorem 2.2(i) (cited from [19]; with the normalization of (2.22)-(2.23), see item :03); Remark 4.2 notes only k-1 can be proved. (ii) follows from Lemma 3.2 (proof p. 553) with condition (3.10) given by Corollary 3.5, which rests on Theorem 3.4 from [10]. The result is for the semidiscrete scheme. The scheme field already includes the ENO reconstruction, so the sentence alone is also TRUE.

sentence: Then uΔx ⇀ u (up to a subsequence) in L2([0,T],L2(R)) as Δx → 0, where u is the unique weak solution of the linear system.

scheme.definition: TeCNO scheme (1.6), (3.8) for f(u) = Au with the two-point entropy conservative flux ~F_{i+1/2} = (1/2)(Au_i + Au_{i+1}) (2.9) (entropy E = (1/2)u^T S u, v = Su), high-order flux ~F^{2p} from (2.20), ENO-reconstructed diffusion; uΔx(x,t) = u_i(t) for x ∈ I_i. In the proof (A symmetric) the diffusion is D = (a/2)I with Δx/(2Δt) ≤ a ≤ Δx/Δt, giving (4.1) F = ~F^{2k} - (a/2)⟨⟨u⟩⟩ with componentwise ENO reconstruction of u.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Linear system f(u) = Au with constant m×m matrix A
There is a symmetric positive definite S with SA symmetric
Scheme with flux (3.8) based on the two-point flux (2.9)
Proof given for symmetric A and Lax-Friedrichs-type diffusion D = (a/2)I

justification: Proof pp. 557-558: the entropy (energy) identity, the sign property (3.17) and the jump bound (3.18) give the uniform L2 bound and entropy production bound (4.2); a weakly convergent subsequence exists, and a Lax-Wendroff-type argument plus Cauchy-Schwarz with (4.2) shows the diffusion term vanishes (≤ C√Δx), so the limit is a weak solution, which is unique for the linear symmetrizable system. The proof treats symmetric A with D = (a/2)I 'for simplicity' and relies on (3.18) from [10]. The sentence names 'the linear system', and constant-coefficient hyperbolic systems with a convex quadratic entropy are symmetrizable, so the dropped hypothesis is harmless; only weak convergence (up to a subsequence) is claimed, and the sentence says so.

sentence: Then, the following L∞ estimate holds: (4.5) a < u_i(T) < b ∀ i ∈ Z, T ≥ 0.

scheme.definition: TeCNO scheme (1.6), (3.8) for a scalar conservation law, built with the convex entropy E(u) = -log(b - u) - log(u - a) (4.4) (entropy variables and entropy conservative flux associated with this entropy).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Scalar conservation law (1.1) with initial data a < u_0(x) < b for all x ∈ R
TeCNO flux (3.8) associated with the entropy (4.4)

justification: Alone: without a < u_0 < b the estimate already fails at T = 0 (u_i(0) = u_0(x_i)), so the dropped hypothesis is needed. With hypotheses: the proof (p. 558) sums the entropy inequality (3.11) over i ∈ Z to get Δx sum_i E(u_i(T)) ≤ Δx sum_i E(u_0(x_i)) and uses the lower bound of E to bound each E(u_i(T)); on a periodic or finite grid this argument works, but on the whole line the sum sum_i E(u_0(x_i)) is in general infinite (E is bounded below by a constant that need not be zero), and the step to the upper bound C_2 is only asserted. Nothing we read closes this gap for data on R.

sentence: The TeCNO scheme (6.4), (6.5) is (i) kth-order accurate for smooth solutions, (ii) entropy stable—computed solutions satisfy (6.9) d/dt E(u_{i,j}) + (1/Δx)(^Q^{x,2p}_{i+1/2,j} − ^Q^{x,2p}_{i−1/2,j}) + (1/Δy)(^Q^{y,2p}_{i,j+1/2} − ^Q^{y,2p}_{i−1/2,j}) ≤ 0 with ^Q^{x,2p}_{i+1/2,j} = ~Q^{x,2p}_{i+1/2,j} − (1/2) v^T_{i+1/2,j} ^D^x_{i+1/2,j} ⟨⟨v⟩⟩_{i+1/2,j}, ^Q^{y,2p}_{i,j+1/2} = ~Q^{y,2p}_{i,j+1/2} − (1/2) v^T_{i,j+1/2} ^D^y_{i,j+1/2} ⟨⟨v⟩⟩_{i,j+1/2}.

scheme.definition: Two-dimensional semidiscrete TeCNO scheme on a Cartesian mesh: d/dt u_{i,j} + (1/Δx)(F_{i+1/2,j} - F_{i-1/2,j}) + (1/Δy)(G_{i,j+1/2} - G_{i,j-1/2}) = 0 (6.4), F_{i+1/2,j} = ~F^{2p}_{i+1/2,j} - (1/2) D^x_{i+1/2,j} ⟨⟨v⟩⟩_{i+1/2,j}, G_{i,j+1/2} = ~G^{2p}_{i,j+1/2} - (1/2) D^y_{i,j+1/2} ⟨⟨v⟩⟩_{i,j+1/2} (6.5); ~F^{2p}, ~G^{2p} from (6.8) with the α of (2.20); ENO reconstruction of entropy variables dimension by dimension along R^x, R^y (Sec. 6.2.2); 2p = k or k+1.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Convex entropy E with entropy fluxes Q^x, Q^y satisfying (6.2)
Two-point entropy conservative fluxes satisfying (6.6); ENO reconstruction dimension by dimension
Integer k ≥ 1, 2p = k (k even) or k+1 (k odd)

justification: (i) claims k-th order, but the proof is only 'analogous to that of Theorem 4.1', which proves (k-1)th order, and Remark 4.2 (p. 556) says a nonzero Δx^{k-1} term in the diffusion operator does not vanish; the experiments show k-th order behaviour in 1D (Fig. 3, p. 560). So (i) is neither proved nor refuted by what we read. (ii) follows dimension by dimension from the 1D argument (Lemma 3.2, Corollary 3.5), but (6.9) as printed writes ^Q^{y,2p}_{i−1/2,j} where ^Q^{y,2p}_{i,j−1/2} is meant, so the printed inequality is not well formed. Both readings UNSURE.

sentence: The schemes do not involve any tuning parameters and are (i) arbitrarily high-order accurate for smooth solutions of (1.1), (ii) entropy stable—they satisfy a discrete entropy inequality (3.11), (iii) essentially nonoscillatory near discontinuities.

scheme.definition: TeCNO schemes (1.6), (3.8) with ENO-reconstructed scaled entropy variables (Sec. 3.5) and ~F^{2p} from (2.20).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Smooth solutions for accuracy; proven order k-1 for k-th order reconstruction
Semidiscrete entropy inequality (3.11)

justification: No tuning parameters: true by construction (pp. 546, 570). (i) TRUE by Theorem 4.1(i) for arbitrary k. (ii) TRUE by Theorem 4.1(ii) (semidiscrete). (iii) 'essentially nonoscillatory near discontinuities' is not proved anywhere in the paper; it is supported only by the experiments (Sec. 5, e.g. p. 561 dam break 'without any noticeable oscillations'), and the term has no precise definition here. The sentence is TRUE only if every part is, so both readings are UNSURE.

sentence: Entropy stability implies that the approximate solutions are bounded in Lp for some p.

scheme.definition: TeCNO schemes (1.6), (3.8), entropy stable in the sense of (3.11).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Summing (3.11) over i (periodic or no-inflow boundaries) gives a discrete version of the entropy bound (1.5)
E convex

justification: Summing (3.11) gives Δx sum_i E(u_i(T)) ≤ Δx sum_i E(u_i(0)). Turning that into an Lp bound needs growth of E (e.g. E(u) ≥ c|u|^p - C), which the paper does not state or prove (p. 545 only says the bound 'can be converted into an a priori estimate ... in suitable Lp spaces [6]'). It works for quadratic entropies (L2, as in Theorem 4.3) and for the log entropy (4.4) (L∞, Lemma 4.4), but for the Euler entropy -ρs/(γ-1) it is not shown. Nothing we read settles the general claim.

sentence: Entropy stability follows as a consequence of the sign property of the ENO reconstruction, shown in a recent paper [10].

scheme.definition: TeCNO schemes (1.6), (3.8) with ENO reconstruction in scaled entropy variables (Sec. 3.5).

hypotheses.hypothesis: D = RΛR^T with R nonsingular, Λ ≥ 0 diagonal
Entropy conservative ~F^{2p}

justification: Lemma 3.2 (proof p. 553) shows that the sign condition (3.10)/(3.12) on the reconstructed jumps gives the entropy inequality (3.11); Corollary 3.5 (p. 556) obtains (3.12) from the ENO sign property, Theorem 3.4, which is quoted from [10]. The implication claimed in the sentence is therefore proved in the paper; the sign property itself is attributed to [10], as the sentence says.

sentence: We also prove that the TeCNO schemes converge for linear symmetrizable systems.

scheme.definition: TeCNO scheme (1.6), (3.8) for f(u) = Au with two-point flux (2.9) and ENO-reconstructed diffusion.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Constant-coefficient linear system with symmetric positive definite S such that SA is symmetric
Convergence is weak in L2([0,T], L2(R)), up to a subsequence, as Δx → 0
Two-point flux (2.9)

justification: With hypotheses: Theorem 4.3 and its proof (pp. 557-558) give weak L2 convergence to the unique weak solution (see item :10); the paper adds (p. 558) that generalizing to smooth variable coefficients is 'straightforward', which is not shown, but the sentence's core case is covered. Alone, 'converge' would usually be read as (strong) convergence of the approximations; the paper proves only weak convergence, and nothing we read settles strong convergence, so UNSURE.

sentence: The main difference between TeCNO schemes and other existing very-high-order schemes lies in the fact that the TeCNO are rigorously proved to be stable.

scheme.definition: TeCNO schemes (1.6), (3.8); compared with other very-high-order schemes (ENO, WENO, DG) as surveyed on pp. 545-546.

hypotheses.hypothesis: 'Stable' means entropy stable (semidiscrete discrete entropy inequality), giving an a priori Lp estimate
Context: systems of conservation laws

justification: The TeCNO part is true in the sense of semidiscrete entropy stability (Theorem 4.1(ii)). The comparative part, that other very-high-order schemes are not proved stable, is a claim about the literature: the paper's own survey (pp. 545-546) cites DG methods with a global entropy estimate for scalar laws [4] and WENO convergence for smooth solutions [16], so the claim holds at best for entropy stability of systems, and 'stable' is not specified. Nothing we read settles it, so both readings are UNSURE.

sentence: In this paper, a new fifth-order weighted essentially non-oscillatory scheme is developed.

scheme.definition: WENO5M: df/dx|_{x_j} ≈ (f^_{j+1/2} - f^_{j-1/2})/Δx (48a), f^_{j±1/2} = sum_{k=0}^{2} ω^(M)_k f^k_{j±1/2} (48b), with candidate fluxes f^0_{j+1/2} = (1/6)(2f_{j-2} - 7f_{j-1} + 11f_j), f^1_{j+1/2} = (1/6)(-f_{j-1} + 5f_j + 2f_{j+1}), f^2_{j+1/2} = (1/6)(2f_j + 5f_{j+1} - f_{j+2}) (15); mapped weights ω^(M)_k = α*_k / sum_i α*_i (46), α*_k = g_k(ω^(JS)_k) (44), g_k(ω) = ω(ω̄_k + ω̄_k^2 - 3ω̄_k ω + ω^2)/(ω̄_k^2 + ω(1 - 2ω̄_k)) (43); ω^(JS)_k = α_k/sum_i α_i, α_k = ω̄_k/(ε + β_k)^p (30), ideal weights ω̄ = 1/10, 6/10, 3/10 (21), smoothness indicators β_k (37); ε = 10^-40 in the tests. Time stepping in tests: third order Runge-Kutta (52).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Smooth solutions; fifth order also near critical points where f' = 0 (first-order critical points)
Order analysis with ε = 0 (ε assumed 0 in the analysis)
For higher-order critical points (n_CP = r-1 = 2 for r = 3, i.e. f' = f'' = 0) the mapping is ineffective and the rate is 2

justification: Alone ('fifth-order' for smooth solutions in general): the paper's own Sec. 6 and Table 10 (pp. 565-566) give rate 2 for the mapped r = 3 scheme at critical points with f' = f'' = 0 (n_CP = 2) and state the mappings are ineffective there, so fifth order does not hold at every point of a smooth solution. With hypotheses (smooth solution, critical points at most first order, ε negligible): Sec. 5.1, eqs. (45)-(47) p. 556-557, give ω^(M)_k = ω̄_k + O(Δx^3) and sum ω^(M)_k = 1, which satisfies the sufficient conditions (25), so the scheme is fifth order even where f' = 0; Tables 4 and 6 confirm rate 5 numerically.

sentence: Necessary and sufficient conditions on the weights for fifth-order convergence are derived; one more condition than previously published is found.

scheme.definition: Class of fifth-order WENO schemes on the three candidate stencils of Fig. 3: f^_{j±1/2} = sum_{k=0}^{2} ω_k f^k_{j±1/2} (12), (22), candidate fluxes (15), ideal weights ω̄ = 1/10, 6/10, 3/10 (21), derivative approximated by (f^_{j+1/2} - f^_{j-1/2})/Δx (6). Conditions (29): sum_k (ω_k - ω̄_k) = O(Δx^6) (29a); (3ω^(+)_1 - 3ω^(-)_1 - ω^(+)_2 + ω^(-)_2 + ω^(+)_3 - ω^(-)_3) = O(Δx^3) (29b, as printed); ω_k - ω̄_k = O(Δx^2) (29c).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Smooth f; Taylor expansions of the candidate fluxes (16)-(17)
Conditions apply to the + and - interface weights; the previous (Jiang-Shu) conditions correspond to (29a) and (29c) only

justification: The conditions (29) are obtained by a formal Taylor-expansion derivation (pp. 549-550) that identifies which error terms must vanish; sufficiency follows from that expansion, but necessity is not proved (no argument rules out cancellation between the remainders), and the paper itself notes on p. 549 that the closely related conditions (25) are sufficient but 'not necessary'. That (29b) is missing from the Jiang-Shu analysis is correct (p. 550; cf. Jiang-Shu (2.14)). Also (29b) as printed indexes weights 1, 2, 3 although k ∈ {0, 1, 2}. Nothing we read settles necessity, so both readings are UNSURE.

sentence: A detailed analysis reveals that the version of this scheme implemented by Jiang and Shu [G.-S. Jiang, C.-W. Shu, Efficient implementation of weighted ENO schemes, J. Comput. Phys. 126 (1996) 202–228] is, in general, only third-order accurate at critical points.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Critical points where f' = 0 and f''' ≠ 0 (f' = O(Δx) near them)
ε assumed 0 in the analysis (ε small relative to β_k); with larger ε the weights approach the ideal ones and the order changes

justification: Sec. 4.2 (pp. 551-552, Table 1, eq. (39)) shows that where f' = 0 the indicators β_0, β_2 are (13/12)(f''Δx^2)^2(1 + O(Δx)), so ω^(JS)_k = ω̄_k + O(Δx), violating (29c), which gives third order; Table 3 (ε = 10^-40, rates ≈ 2.99 at x = 0 for f = x^3 + cos x) and Table 8 (L∞ rate ≈ 3.27) confirm it. 'In general' in the sentence covers the ε caveat: Sec. 4.3 and Fig. 7 show that once a fixed ε dominates β_k the scheme tends to the fifth-order upstream central scheme, so the third order is seen only while ε is small relative to the indicators; on the formal (ε → 0) reading used throughout the paper, the sentence holds as stated.

sentence: The magnitude of ε, a parameter which keeps the weights bounded, and the level of grid resolution are shown to determine the order of the scheme in a non-trivial way.

scheme.definition: WENO5 of Jiang and Shu, (41) with weights (30) and indicators (37), parameter ε > 0 in α_k = ω̄_k/(ε + β_k)^p.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Smooth solution with critical points (f' = 0, f''' ≠ 0); comparison over ε ∈ {10^-40, 10^-15, 10^-6} and grids Δx from 10^-3 down
hypotheses.location: pp. 553-555, Sec. 4.5, Tables 2-3; pp. 559-561, Tables 7-8, Fig. 7

justification: Eq. (40b) (p. 553) shows α_k = ω̄_k/(ε + f'^2Δx^2 + O(Δx^4)), so the weights, and hence the local error, depend on the ratio of ε to the indicators, which shrink with Δx; Table 3 (p. 555) gives rates near 3 for ε = 10^-40, rates rising from 3 to 6.5 for ε = 10^-15, and rates 6-7 for ε = 10^-6 at the same grids, and Fig. 7 (p. 560) shows WENO5 curves moving from the third-order to the fifth-order envelope as Δx decreases. This is an analytical observation backed by computations; it holds both alone and with hypotheses.

sentence: A simple modification of the original scheme is found to be sufficient to give optimal order convergence even near critical points.

scheme.definition: WENO5M (48): Jiang-Shu weights ω^(JS)_k (30), (37) mapped by g_k(ω) = ω(ω̄_k + ω̄_k^2 - 3ω̄_k ω + ω^2)/(ω̄_k^2 + ω(1 - 2ω̄_k)) (43), α*_k = g_k(ω^(JS)_k) (44), ω^(M)_k = α*_k / sum_i α*_i (46); candidate fluxes (15).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Critical points where f' = 0 (with f'' ≠ 0, i.e. n_CP = 1); for n_CP = r-1 the mapping is ineffective
Analysis with ε = 0; holds even for very small ε (10^-40 in tests)
Smooth solution

justification: Alone ('near critical points', any order of critical point): Sec. 6 and Table 10 (pp. 565-566) of the same paper give rate 2 for the mapped fifth-order scheme (r = 3) at critical points with f' = f'' = 0 (n_CP = 2), noting the mapping is ineffective when n_CP = r-1; so optimal order is not reached near every critical point. With hypotheses (first-order critical points, f' = 0, smooth solution): eqs. (45)-(47) (pp. 556-557) give ω^(M)_k = ω̄_k + O(Δx^3), satisfying (25), hence fifth order; Table 4 (rates → 4.98) and Table 6 (rates ≈ 5.00 in L1, L2, L∞) confirm it with ε = 10^-40.

sentence: It has been shown that the previously published constraints for fifth-order accurate WENO schemes are incomplete.

scheme.definition: Class of fifth-order WENO schemes on the three candidate stencils (12), (15), (21); previously published constraints are sum ω_k = 1 and ω_k = ω̄_k + O(Δx^2) (Jiang-Shu (2.14) with r = 3), i.e. (29a) and (29c) only.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Smooth solution; accuracy judged on the flux difference (f^_{j+1/2} - f^_{j-1/2})/Δx rather than on each flux

justification: Expanding the flux difference (26) (p. 550) leaves the term Δx^3 sum_k A_k (ω^(+)_k - ω^(-)_k) with A_k ≠ 0 from (16); constraints (29a) and (29c) alone allow ω^(+)_k - ω^(-)_k = O(Δx^2), which leaves an O(Δx^5) error in the flux difference, i.e. an O(Δx^4) derivative error, so an extra condition (29b) is needed (p. 550: 'Eq. (29b) is not presented there and thus the constraints presented in [1] are incomplete'). This follows directly from the source's own expansion.

sentence: The extensions to higher orders are similarly afflicted near critical points.

scheme.definition: Higher-order WENO schemes ((2r-1)th order from r-th order ENO stencils, up to 11th order) with Jiang-Shu-type weights; not defined in this source; outlined in Balsara and Shu [9] as cited on pp. 543 and 565.
scheme.location: not defined in this source; defined in D. Balsara, C.-W. Shu [9] as cited on p. 565

hypotheses.hypothesis: Taylor analysis under the assumption ε = 0, r ≤ 6
Near critical points of order n_CP ≥ 1

justification: Sec. 6 (p. 565) states that 'it is easily verified' by Taylor analysis (with ε = 0) that the higher-order schemes lose 2 orders at n_CP = 1 and more at higher-order critical points, and gives the rate formula (60) 'inferring from the results' plus Table 10; no derivation is shown, so the support is a sketch. With fixed ε > 0 the weights tend to the ideal ones as Δx → 0 (p. 553 for the fifth-order case), so the loss depends on ε and resolution. Nothing else we read settles the higher-order case.

sentence: Former algorithms for finding these weights do not satisfy this incomplete set of criteria in the neighborhood of critical points and, in the worst case, result in (r − 1)th order convergence for smooth flows.

scheme.definition: WENO schemes with Jiang-Shu weights (30) and indicators of the form (35)/(37) and their higher-order extensions (r up to 6, Balsara-Shu [9], not defined in this source).
scheme.location: eqs. (30) p. 551, (35)-(37) pp. 551-552; higher orders as cited on p. 565

hypotheses.hypothesis: ε = 0 in the analysis
Worst case is a critical point of order n_CP = r-1; rate formula (60) for r ≤ 6
Smooth flow

justification: First part: for r = 3 Sec. 4.2 (eq. (39), p. 552) shows ω^(JS)_k = ω̄_k + O(Δx) near critical points, so (29c) fails; this is derived. Second part: the worst-case rate r-1 comes from formula (60) and Table 10 (pp. 565-566: r = 3, n_CP = 2 gives 2; r = 6, n_CP = 5 gives 5), which the authors infer from Taylor analysis that is not shown ('easily verified', 'inferring from the results'). Since the sentence is TRUE only if both parts hold and the second rests on an unshown analysis, both readings are UNSURE.

sentence: A correction is given which achieves the full (2r − 1)th order accuracy in the neighborhood of critical points where f' = 0, even for very small ε.

scheme.definition: Mapped WENO: weights ω^(JS)_k mapped by g_k (43), α*_k = g_k(ω^(JS)_k) (44), normalized (46), applied once or twice (Sec. 6); for r = 3 this is WENO5M (48).

hypotheses.hypothesis: Critical points with 1 ≤ n_CP < r-1; for n_CP = r-1 the mappings are ineffective
One or two applications of the mapping (Table 10)
ε = 0 analysis; ε = 10^-40 in the tests

justification: Alone: Table 10 (p. 566) of the same paper shows the mapped schemes do not reach 2r-1 at critical points with n_CP = r-1 (e.g. r = 3, n_CP = 2: rate 2; r = 4, n_CP = 3: rate 3), all of which have f' = 0; with one mapping r = 4, n_CP = 2 gives 6, not 7. With hypotheses: for r = 3 and n_CP = 1 the claim is derived (eqs. (45)-(47), pp. 556-557) and confirmed (Tables 4, 6); for general r with 1 ≤ n_CP < r-1 the paper only says it 'is predicted' (p. 565) from Table 10, with no derivation shown. Since the sentence is about general r, the hypothesis reading is UNSURE.

justification: Alone ('true fifth-order ... when approximating smooth solutions', all smooth solutions): Table 10 and Sec. 6 (pp. 565-566) give rate 2 for the mapped fifth-order scheme at critical points with f' = f'' = 0, so fifth order fails for some smooth solutions. With hypotheses (critical points at most first order): fifth order follows from (45)-(47) and Tables 4, 6; the second clause is supported by Table 9 (both methods converge at rates 0.82-1.03, WENO5M errors about 10% lower) and by the bound of at most first order for captured discontinuities (pp. 564-565, refs [18], [19]).

justification: For discontinuous solutions a captured discontinuity is smeared over at least one cell, so the L1 error is at least of order Δx and the rate cannot exceed one; the paper cites that nominally fifth-order schemes converge at about 5/6 order in L1 for linearly degenerate discontinuities ([18], [19], p. 565). Table 9 (p. 565) measures rates of 0.82-1.03 for both schemes on the Sod problem. The sentence already restricts itself to flows with discontinuities ('in both cases').
